💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral.
  • Recent findings suggest that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team.
  • Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, mistral Large 4 (aka Le Chonk) is a multimodal, multilingual, Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) model from Mistral. It takes text and images as input and generates text. It has about 1T total, 49B active parameter, and a context window of 1M tokens.

The model is released in two official variants:.

Recent findings suggest that there are also GGUFs created by Unsloth and the llama.cpp team. It’s distributed under the Mistral Ecosystem Open-Weight License (an MIT derivative that establishes limitations for model-as-a-service offerings).

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4 is particularly strong for cybersecurity, coding agents, and multimodality. In this post, we look at how the model works, its capabilities, architecture and more!

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 combines a large pool of experts with sparse attention and a Pixtral vision encoder. The language model selects a small group of experts for each token, while its attention indexer selects which earlier token positions to attend to. These are two different forms of sparsity, where one selects feed-forward networks, the other selects context positions.

You can find all the checkpoints in the Mistral Large 4 collection.

In a recent development, mistral Large 4 scores 82% on the Artificial Analysis Cyber Index test that asks a model to reproduce a real vulnerability in open-source software and then patch the software. Mistral reports that several closed frontier models score near zero on the same test because they refuse to attempt the work. This is super key for defenders, because fixing a vulnerability usually requires reproducing the vulnerability. In Mistral’s internal testing, Mistral Large 4 was also useful for malware analysis, vulnerability prioritisation and writing detection rules, which the model was not explicitly trained for.

Mistral mainly positions the model for defensive security work. Vulnerability research and incident response often appear like attacks in model input, so closed source filters can block them. A team that depends on an API can also lose access in the middle of an incident. Crucially, open weight models put both the usage policy and the deployment under the user’s control. That said, the model still declines harmful requests: on cyber prompts from JailbreakBench, StrongREJECT and AgentHarm, its average refusal rate is higher than any other open weight model.

According to recent reports, for community builders, an open weight model like Mistral Large 4 unlocks a load of downstream use cases. You could build your own cyber system around your code base, crash logs, and malware samples. For example, with TRL you could fine-tune smaller models from Mistral Large 4 traces patching your code base. In fact, reproduce-then-patch tasks use a verifiable reward, so it fits with RL environments that could be used to further RL smaller security models. Open weights also let researchers measure the model’s refusal behaviour directly instead of relying on the provider’s description.

In short, cyber capabilities like ML4’s in the open are a huge boost for the community.

We have interviewed Pierre Stock about the cyber capabilities of the model, you can watch it here.

Industry observers note that mistral Large 4’s text decoder has 72 layers, a hidden dimension of 6,144, and 64 attention heads. Its attention blocks combine Multi-head Latent Attention (MLA) with a DeepSeek Sparse Attention (DSA) indexer (a direction in other models such as GLM 5.3). MLA keeps a compressed KV representation, and DSA selects up to 2,048 key positions for each query.

For each decoder block, there’s a 3:1 RoPE to NoPE pattern, i.e. 3 decoder layers employ RoPE and every fourth layer uses NoPE. The model also shares KV state across layers.The first decoder layer uses a dense feed-forward network. The other 71 layers use MoE blocks, in which a softmax router selects four of the 128 experts for each token. One shared expert always runs alongside the selected experts, for a total of 5 active experts per token.

Regarding RoPE, Mistral uses LeRope, a YaRN-scaled RoPE with one learned multiplier per frequency.

It has been revealed that mistral Large 4 employs a 1.6B Pixtral encoder. Pixtral has 30 layers, a hidden dimension of 2,048, and 16 attention heads. It uses 14 × 14 patches and a patch-merge projector with spatial merge size 2. You can see the encoder pipeline below.

Mistral Large 4 delivers strong benchmark performance across coding, cybersecurity, multimodal understanding, and agentic workflows, positioning it as a competitive addition to the open-weight ecosystem. As of October 29, 2026, the model is the fifth best open weights model on Artificial Analysis Intelligence index.

On coding, ML4 achieves 61.7% on DeepSWE v1.1, 59.4% on SWE-Atlas-QnA, and 28.3% on Terminal-Bench 4. Its combined Coding Agent Index score of 49.8% places it ahead of DeepSeek V4 Pro 0813 and Qwen3.8 Max.

Coding capabilities of ML4 extend to knowledge work, with 59.9% on AutomationBench and 1,393 Elo on AA-Briefcase, which evaluate business workflows and long-horizon professional tasks.

Cybersecurity is one of Mistral Large 4’s standout capabilities, with strong results across real-world vulnerability assessment and security competition tasks. Three benchmarks highlight the model’s cyber performance:.

Sources indicate that mistral Large 4 also demonstrates 93.3% attack resistance on Lakera’s B3 benchmark, adding evidence of robustness against prompt-injection attacks. Beyond benchmarks, internal testing showed promising results in malware analysis, vulnerability prioritization, and detection-rule generation.

Mistral Large 4 is shipped with day-0 support for transformers, vLLM and llama.cpp. GGUF quants are available from GGUF and the llama.cpp team. We provide options to deploy remotely with Inference Endpoints, and use serverless inference through Inference Providers.

The Transformers implementation provides AutoModelForMultimodalLM, with AutoProcessor preparing the conversation and image inputs. Mistral Large 4 can take low, medium, high as reasoning effort. The default is high, and note that reasoning cannot be disabled, so using reasoning_effort: none would still use high.

Safe Autoformalization: Sufficiency and Necessity with Entailment Graphs

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (309 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Recent findings suggest that arXiv:2611.31571v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Autoformalization translates a natural-language statement into a formula that captures its intent, which depends on the statement's context: the background that disambiguates it. LLMs make autoformalization practical, but their probabilistic output carries no formal guarantees. We propose techniques for safe autoformalization that certify one-sided logical adequacy: a formula sufficient for the intent is safe to enforce, and a formula necessary for it is safe to rely on. We use LLMs to generate candidate formulas and order them by logical strength in an Entailment Graph (EG), an ordering a solver decides. Each edge carries a residual and a co-residual, the two adjoints of the entailment order, all fixed by the candidate pool alone. In a context, two searches return the sufficient frontier, the weakest candidates that entail the statement, and the necessary frontier, the strongest candidates the statement entails; each step is one local check against an edge's residual or co-residual. The frontiers bracket the statement and yield the ambiguity residue, which holds exactly of the situations the candidates certify neither as satisfying nor as violating it; the statement is ambiguous precisely when the residue is satisfiable. For natural-language statements and contexts, an LLM entailment oracle decides the checks; it is sound if it accepts only checks that hold, and complete if it accepts every check that holds. We prove that a sound oracle makes the search safe regardless of pool quality, and that a complete one makes the frontiers tight. On security-critical AWS properties, EGs are safe in all 20 cases of an expert-adjudicated study, where majority vote over equivalence clusters and Universal Self-Consistency are unsafe in 25% and 10%. An ablation with the same oracle but no graph is unsafe in 25% and rejects every candidate in another 30%. We machine-checked our proofs in Lean.

Breaking: Optimize AI economics on Amazon Bedrock with Accenture’s sequenced approach

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1979 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • In a recent development, as enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall.
  • In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.
  • Industry observers note that accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In a recent development, as enterprises scale AI on Amazon Bedrock, token spend often grows even as per-token prices fall. Without cost allocation tags in place, your cloud invoice reveals AI spend as a single line item rather than by team, workload, agent, or model. Cheaper tokens expand adoption, and agentic workloads multiply invocations. As successful AI use cases scale, consumption can rise faster than unit prices drop. The economic question is whether the business value generated grows faster than the cost of the intelligence required to produce it. The Linux Foundation has introduced the Tokenomics Foundation to develop open standards for AI cost economics, a sign that managing the economics of AI is now an industry discipline.

In this post, you will learn about six levers for optimizing token spend, how Accenture applied them in production, and how to apply them using Amazon Bedrock.

Industry observers note that accenture applied these levers in four client engagements across telecom, insurance, mining, and a large enterprise deployment. The same levers are available natively on Amazon Bedrock as described in this post. Where savings were measured, token spend fell by about 40–85 percent. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary. Client names are withheld by Accenture to protect client confidentiality.

It has been revealed that before you optimize anything, you need to see where consumption is occurring, who owns it, and what business value it produces. Cost allocation tags at the team, workload, and agent level are the prerequisite for connecting consumption to accountable owners and, ultimately, to business outcomes. You apply them through Amazon Bedrock application inference profiles, one profile per application or workload, tagged by team, cost center, and environment. After you activate them as cost allocation tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console, you can use these tags to trace which teams, applications, and agents are driving spend. They also make it possible to measure the impact of each change you introduce.

Three AWS services provide the underlying telemetry. AWS Cost and Usage Reports (CUR 2.0), delivered through AWS Data Exports, handle financial attribution, breaking down billed inference cost by workload and team after your cost allocation tags are active. Amazon CloudWatch captures operational signals such as invocation counts and latency. Amazon Bedrock model invocation logging records request-level detail, including the model used and the input and output token counts for each call.

It has been revealed that telemetry alone isn’t enough. Engineers can read cost per invocation on a dashboard, but product owners and program leaders need a metric expressed in business terms. Accenture’s Cost per Business Transaction (CpBT) framework bridges this gap. CpBT aggregates all the model invocations, retries, tool calls, and agent handoffs that contribute to one successful business output into a single fully loaded cost figure. It surfaces the true cost of producing a result, including the failed attempts that raw token pricing hides. Tracked against the business value each workflow delivers, CpBT distinguishes a growing bill that reflects scaling success from one that reflects waste.

According to recent reports, the goal of these six levers isn’t to minimize tokens at all costs. It’s to use the right amount and level of intelligence to deliver each business outcome at the appropriate cost, quality, and risk. The levers are organized into three phases based on the complexity of the change and the investment it requires. AWS and Accenture recommend working through the phases in order, and you can apply each phase independently to the workloads where it will have the most impact.

With Amazon Bedrock prompt caching, the model reuses the parts of a prompt that repeat across requests, such as system instructions, tool definitions, and reference documents, so you stop paying full price to process the same content again. Amazon Bedrock stores the key-value state of previously computed prompt prefixes and is designed to skip recomputation on later requests. This is designed to reduce cached input token costs by up to 90 percent for supported models (see Amazon Bedrock Prompt Caching).

Amazon Bedrock batch inference processes non-urgent workloads asynchronously as a group at 50 percent lower cost than on-demand pricing for select models (see Amazon Bedrock Pricing). You submit inference requests as a batch job, and results are written to Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) when processing completes. Batch inference suits nightly reports, document processing pipelines, and evaluation runs that don’t need an immediate response.

Recent findings suggest that both levers add configuration to your existing setup. Prompt caching requires cache checkpoint markers in your prompts, and batch inference requires submitting eligible requests as a batch job instead of calling the on-demand API. Apply caching to interactive, on-demand traffic and batch inference to asynchronous work. Neither requires new infrastructure or architecture changes.

Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing directs requests across models within the same family, matching each task to the level of intelligence its business value, complexity, and risk require, rather than defaulting every request to the most powerful model. Intelligent prompt routing can reduce costs by up to 30 percent without compromising accuracy (see Amazon Bedrock intelligent prompt routing). Check Amazon Bedrock Pricing for any routing charges. In the following engagements, Accenture’s model tiering and triage routing apply this same routing lever.

According to recent reports, retrieval Augmented Generation (RAG) optimization tunes the retrieval step in the RAG process so that fewer unnecessary context tokens reach the model. Techniques such as hierarchical chunking, metadata-based filtering, and reranking narrow the retrieved context to the most relevant chunks, so you pay primarily for content that improves the answer.

Sources indicate that two complementary Accenture patterns work alongside these AWS native levers. Context scoping limits the data each agent receives to the document slice relevant to its step of the workflow, rather than passing the full case context at every handoff. Context compression summarizes or filters documents before they reach the model. Both reduce input token volume, especially across multi-agent chains.

According to recent reports, semantic caching stores responses and reuses them when a latest request is semantically similar to one already answered, even if the wording differs. This avoids redundant model invocations and reduces both cost and latency. On AWS, you can implement it with a vector store such as Amazon ElastiCache in front of the model. In an AWS benchmark on 63,796 real chatbot queries, a 0.90 similarity threshold produced a 74.5 percent cache hit rate, 92.3 percent accuracy, and 72.5 percent cost savings (see ElastiCache semantic caching benchmarks). As you apply routing and semantic caching, keep Amazon Bedrock Guardrails on every route, and set semantic cache expiry so that consumers don’t receive outdated answers.

Recent findings suggest that model distillation transfers knowledge from a large teacher model to a smaller, faster student model. Distilled models in Amazon Bedrock are up to 500 percent faster and up to 75 percent less expensive than original models, with less than 2 percent accuracy loss for use cases such as RAG. Distillation is best suited to stable, high-volume workloads where the transaction volume justifies the training investment.

Accenture applied these levers in four client engagements. Each engagement targeted a different cost pattern. In two of them, Accenture applied several changes together, so those results reflect the combined effect rather than any single lever.

The first engagement was a large enterprise deployment where every request went to a frontier model, with no caching, model tiering, or batching. Accenture applied three changes together: model tiering to match each task to the smallest model that could handle it well, prompt caching for repeated context, and batch processing for overnight and non-urgent jobs. Together they cut monthly token cost by 85 percent, and the saving was not separated by change. About 15 percent of tasks still needed the top model for hard, open-ended reasoning, and the rest ran on lighter models. Your split will depend on your workload composition.

The second engagement was a telecom operator with $12 million in annual token spend. Most of that spend came from agents fanning out requests without limits and from every request going to a frontier model regardless of complexity. Accenture applied triage routing, semantic caching, and context compression together. Input tokens fell by 70 percent, and annual token spend fell from $12 million to $3.8 million, a 68 percent reduction. Accenture validated output quality against the operator’s pre-change performance benchmarks.

According to recent reports, the third and fourth engagements each applied a single cache layer. An insurer used model-layer prefix caching, reusing the static portions of its prompts across invocations. A mining operator used an application-layer semantic cache, returning stored responses for repeated queries before they reached the model. Across the two engagements, token spend fell by about 40 percent combined, without model routing changes or training investment.

Outcomes ranged from about 40 percent to about 85 percent, reflecting each client’s starting point. The large enterprise deployment began with no optimization in place and reached 85 percent. The telecom operator reached 68 percent on $12 million in annual token spend, and the insurer and mining operator reached about 40 percent combined with one caching lever each. Results are specific to each client’s workload and may vary.

In a recent development, these savings aren’t the end goal. They create capacity to scale AI workloads, reinvest in higher-value use cases, and improve the return generated by each dollar of AI consumption. Two of these engagements applied several changes at once. When you apply one lever at a time, you can attribute each result to a specific change. AWS and Accenture recommend this sequence for your own workloads: connect consumption to owners and outcomes, apply one lever at a time, measure cost, quality, and business value, and build on what works.

Optimizing AI economics in production requires an ongoing governance cycle spanning cost, quality, risk, and business value, not a one-time technical change. Before you apply any lever, establish a quantitative baseline for both cost and quality so that you can measure the impact of each change against a known starting point. When you validate output quality, use held-out evaluation sets drawn from your actual production traffic rather than synthetic benchmarks. Apply one lever at a time per workload so that you can attribute results to a specific change and roll back cleanly if quality drops below your acceptable thresholds. If you operate in a regulated industry such as financial services, insurance, or healthcare, document your quality test results and rollback procedures as part of your standard change management record.

Industry observers note that these four tenets apply regardless of which levers you are using or what phase of the sequencing you are in. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore is an environment where you can build, connect, and optimize agents at scale with any framework or model. It includes AgentCore Evaluations, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore that provides batch evaluation to support your quality validation cycle as you progress through more advanced levers.

You can begin with three steps. First, turn on cost attribution for Amazon Bedrock by applying cost allocation tags at the team and workload level so that your spend is traceable from day one. Second, activate those tags in the AWS Billing and Cost Management console. Then use CUR 2.0 and model invocation logging to identify high-consumption workloads, and assess each one based on spend, business value, quality requirements, risk, volume, and optimization potential. Third, apply Amazon Bedrock prompt caching to that workload’s interactive traffic and Amazon Bedrock batch inference to its asynchronous jobs as configuration-only changes, and measure the result before you move to architectural changes in Phase 2.

The AWS Well-Architected Agentic AI Lens includes model invocation and token cost optimization (AGENTCOST02), a focus area within the cost optimization pillar for agentic workloads. This focus area provides a structured framework you can use to apply these levers at scale across your organization.

arXiv:2611.31570v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In playtesting games, a human operator is typically required to test most gameplay elements. In this work we present Buddy, an autonomous game solving agent which can solve long time horizon objectives in an unseen 3D role-playing game using off-the-shelf language model systems. Buddy will take actions, receive feedback on those actions, and pursue a goal across many turns. No written walkthrough or model training of any kind is required, and we show that this paradigm holds in a novel environment where the agent must discover solutions via exploration rather than recalling them from pretraining. We demonstrate three downstream capabilities: game solving with no provided walkthrough, logging bug tickets for encountered difficulties, and conversion of successful agent traces into scripted hierarchical task networks for regression testing. Unlike existing playtesting solutions, our framework is fully modular: language models and harnesses can be easily swapped out as capabilities improve over time.

#10249. Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1303 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Announcing Project ProtoStar: Making Publicly Funded Science AI-Ready

📅 29 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.
  • According to recent reports, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research.
  • The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An initiative bringing together universities, research organizations, industry, and the open science community to make publicly funded research easier to discover, reuse, and build upon.

According to recent reports, today, we're announcing Project ProtoStar, an initiative to unlock the potential of publicly funded scientific research by making datasets, models, and code more accessible and reusable, particularly for AI-driven research. ProtoStar brings together research institutions, industry, and the open science community to support the release of scientific artifacts in AI-ready, machine-actionable formats, and to demonstrate their value through a series of open challenges. The first challenge, hosted by Carnegie Mellon University, opens on November 2. See How to Participate below.

The initiative's founding partners include Carnegie Mellon University, Purdue University, Georgia Institute of Technology, Arizona State University, and The George Washington University, all working through the Open Forum for AI (OFAI) as the university coalition partner; the Astera Institute; Hugging Face as the infrastructure partner; and the Open Research Community Accelerator (ORCA), through its Fostering Innovation Network, as the community partner.

In a recent development, participating organizations formalize their involvement through a memorandum of understanding supporting the release of suitable scientific datasets, models, and code in AI-ready formats on open infrastructure. Organizations interested in joining Project ProtoStar can reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

The U.S. federal government invests approximately $190 billion annually in research and development, and federal policy increasingly expects the results to be shared publicly. Agencies such as the National Institutes of Health (NIH) and National Science Foundation (NSF) have strengthened public-access requirements for funded research publications and require researchers to plan for sharing the underlying data. Hugging Face is among the ten generalist repositories listed by NIH for sharing research data.

Sources indicate that but making research publicly available does not automatically make it usable. Scientific datasets, models, and code are often scattered across incompatible systems, stored in static or legacy formats, or released without the documentation, metadata, and provenance needed to understand and reuse them. These limitations make it harder for researchers to build on existing work, and harder still for AI systems to discover, interpret, and combine scientific resources across disciplines.

It has been revealed that project ProtoStar aims to help close this gap by encouraging systematic sharing of publicly funded scientific artifacts in AI-ready formats, supported by open infrastructure and practical publishing guidance. It builds on efforts such as the National Cancer Institute's AI Data-Readiness Challenge and Hugging Face's guide to preparing public-sector data for AI. The goal is to make it easier for research organizations to meet existing public-access expectations while increasing the scientific value of the work they release.

The demand for reusable scientific resources is already evident. Hugging Face hosts more than 17,000 public datasets across core scientific domains, including genomics, protein design, chemistry, weather and climate, Earth observation, and astronomy. That figure approaches 29,000 when medicine and mathematics are included, alongside a comparable number of scientific models.

The pace of sharing is also accelerating. Researchers shared more than three times as many new science datasets on Hugging Face in the first nine months of 2026 as in the same period of 2025, with growth remaining substantial even after excluding the largest individual uploader.

Figure 1. Upcoming public science datasets on Hugging Face per quarter, by domain (Q1 2023–Q3 2026). Counts datasets still public, by creation date. Source: Hugging Face Hub data, October 2026. Explore the data.

According to recent reports, when organizations share research in reusable formats, the scientific community can build on it at scale. The 18 public repositories maintained by NIH's National Center for Biotechnology Information (NCBI) on Hugging Face have collectively received more than 11 million downloads, while NASA IMPACT's 27 repositories have received approximately 770,000 downloads, as of October 26, 2026. Documentation is also an key part of making these resources useful: 90% of dataset downloads on Hugging Face are from fully documented datasets.

Recent findings suggest that publicly available genomic data has proved crucial in contributing to research that further advances fields such as biological research; researchers at Hugging Face have been building on openly available scientific resources, including recent releases from HuggingFaceBio such as Carbon-A and Carbon-X. By releasing the resulting models, datasets, and tools openly, these efforts demonstrate how existing scientific resources can support latest research that others can build upon.

This is the kind of activity that we are further catalyzing via Project ProtoStar through institutional policies adopted by participating orgs. As an early example of institutional commitment, CMU's Open Source Programs Office is encouraging its researchers to share suitable datasets, AI models, and other research outputs on Hugging Face, while recognizing the continued importance of domain-specific repositories.

Industry observers note that making scientific artifacts AI-ready is an important first step. We also want to demonstrate what researchers, developers, and the broader scientific community can accomplish when those resources are made available for reuse.

A central question for ProtoStar is: Can publicly funded scientific datasets, models, and code, released in AI-ready formats, be readily discovered, reused, combined, and extended to accelerate scientific discovery and public benefit?

To explore this, ProtoStar will organize a series of open challenges, each hosted by a participating research institution and built around scientific resources that the institution has released openly. The challenges have two complementary goals:.

The resulting projects and lessons learned will help build a practical evidence base for making publicly funded science more accessible and useful.

Hosted by Carnegie Mellon University | November 2–13, 2026.

It has been revealed that the inaugural ProtoStar challenge invites participants to test whether AI can improve predictions of urban climate conditions using historical weather data from 210 U.S. cities. Building on research by Carnegie Mellon University, teams will use climate records through 2018 to predict actual conditions from 2019 to 2026, allowing their models to be evaluated against observed weather rather than hypothetical future scenarios.

In a recent development, participants will forecast four indicators relevant to urban planning: average annual temperature, total annual precipitation, the hottest day of the year, and cooling degree days, a measure of demand for air conditioning. Their predictions will be compared against simple statistical baselines, including historical averages and linear trends, to assess whether AI approaches offer meaningful improvements in accuracy.

Beyond forecasting, participants will also propose a short climate adaptation policy idea informed by what they learned from the data. This component encourages teams to connect scientific analysis with practical public benefits, such as preparing cities for extreme heat, improving energy efficiency, or managing changing precipitation patterns.

Teams will submit a Hugging Face dataset with these outputs. Forecasting performance will be assessed through a public leaderboard measuring prediction errors against established baselines, while policy ideas will receive separate consideration. Final forecasting results will be published in early 2027, once the complete 2026 weather records are available.

Explore the CMU Climate Risk Intelligence Challenge.

It has been revealed that the CMU challenge is the first in this series. Other participating institutions will host their own challenges sequentially, each highlighting different publicly funded scientific resources and opportunities for reuse. Future challenges will be declared through the Project ProtoStar page on Hugging Face.

Whether you're an academic researcher, student, independent developer, or manufacturer building on open scientific infrastructure, ProtoStar offers opportunities to put publicly funded research to work and help us learn what is needed to make AI-ready open science more widely useful.

We also welcome universities, federal research agencies, national laboratories, nonprofits, and other research organizations interested in making their scientific resources more accessible and reusable. To explore participation or collaboration, reach out to protostar@orcaopen.org.

Our hope is that ProtoStar will make it easier for publicly funded scientific work to reach the people and tools that can build on it, while generating practical evidence about the infrastructure and practices needed to support open science at scale.

#10247. COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (192 w)

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

COGENT: A Modular Cognitive Architecture for Agentic User Simulation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (192 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2611.31559v1 Announce Type: upcoming Abstract: LLM-based user simulation can support interface design, accessibility research, and interactive-agent evaluation, but standard computer-use agents are optimized for task completion rather than reproducing how people perceive, reason, and act. We introduce COGENT (COGnitive agENT), a modular cognitive architecture for simulating user interaction with desktop interfaces. COGENT draws on established cognitive theories, such as Norman's action cycle and ACT-R, to enable explainable, intervenable, and modular user simulation by decomposing the simulation process into cognitive modules with explicit representations of perception, memory, user state, intentions, and action selection. We begin by presenting six intervenability demonstrations, each tracing how a single edit to memory, a user attribute, or a processing module propagates through the cognitive pipeline to produce a behavioral change. We evaluate COGENT's behavioral and attributional fidelity across three benchmarks -- AgentNetBench, A11y-CUA, and SENSE-42 -- finding that it achieves statistically significant fidelity gains over computer-use baselines in reproducing recorded human behavior and recovers the relational structure among human self-reported psychological states. Together, these demos and evaluations demonstrate COGENT's utility toward more faithful, explainable, intervenable, and modular LLM-based cognitive simulations.

Amazon Polly debuts voice cloning: A unique voice for your brand

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1390 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release.
  • Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region.
  • Industry observers note that with this newly introduced feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Voice cloning in Amazon Polly is now generally available as a gated release. Give Amazon Polly a few minutes of audio recordings from a speaker who has agreed to have their voice cloned, and Amazon Polly builds your own cloned voice in that speaker’s voice. The cloned voices run on the Amazon Polly generative engine, which delivers similar naturalness and accuracy as the rest of the generative voices. Amazon Polly voice cloning debuts with seven languages: English, Spanish, German, French, Italian, Portuguese, and Hindi. Each cloned voice speaks the language it was recorded in. The cloned voices are automatically encrypted and access-controlled: only you can access your cloned voices.

Amazon Polly voice cloning is available in all the AWS Regions supported by the Amazon Polly generative engine, including the AWS GovCloud (US) Region. Access is already enabled for select Amazon Polly customers. Others can reach out to their AWS account team or apply for access to get access.

Industry observers note that with this newly introduced feature addition, you can build the cloning lifecycle into AWS applications. Building a cloned voice is free for Amazon Polly customers, and Amazon Polly charges for cloned voice usage on a pay-as-you-go basis, see Amazon Polly Pricing page for details.

Press play: the first few seconds are a real recording of the speaker, and then their cloned voice takes over with words they never recorded.

A consistent brand voice across channels.

It has been revealed that establish one recognizable voice and use it across your interactive voice response (IVR) system, cascaded voice agents, mobile app, in-store announcements, advertising, and connected devices. Rather than relying on a generic stock voice or re-booking a recording session each time a script changes, you can generate on-brand audio on demand, with a consistent sound in every channel.

Deliver a distinctive, on-brand voice across self-service flows, and patch prompts as offers and policies change without a upcoming studio session. You can create prompts from source text, test them before rollout, and use the same voice across greeting, routing, and notification experiences.

Creators, publishers, and studios can create audiobooks, courses, podcasts, game characters, and videos in multiple custom voices to enhance the listening experience, and produce subsequent chapters or updates quickly.

Localization with a consistent persona.

Maintain a recognizable voice identity across a content library, so narration remains coherent across titles and updates. Each cloned voice speaks only the language it was recorded in. For multilingual experiences, create and review approved voices per supported language.

Accessibility and personalization.

In a recent development, offer a natural, human-sounding voice for reading experiences, assistive tools, and personalized interactions. You confirm the speaker’s consent each time you create a voice.

With voice cloning, you can build a custom Amazon Polly voice from recordings of a single speaker and then synthesize speech in that voice through the Amazon Polly generative engine. The voice moves through four steps, from recording the speaker to using the finished voice:.

Figure 1: The voice cloning lifecycle, from recording a speaker to using the finished voice.

A cloned voice goes through four steps:.

Sources indicate that A cloned voice is made from one person’s recordings. You confirm that you have the speaker’s consent for all recordings and that you control who can use the voice and when it’s deleted.

For details on intended uses and limitations, see the Amazon Polly AI Service Card and the AWS Responsible Use of AI guidance.

Your cloned voice learns from the recording, including the parts you’d rather it didn’t: the laptop fan, the room echo, the meeting app’s noise filter.

Industry observers note that on the console: once voice cloning is enabled for your account (see Availability), expand the left panel and choose Voice cloning, upload up to 10 recordings or select them from Amazon S3, confirm the terms, and choose Create. Each upload can be up to 5 MB. When the voice is ready, try it out on its details page.

If Python reports that the Polly object has no attribute create_voice, upgrade boto3.

For long texts such as audiobook chapters or course modules, use an asynchronous synthesis task that writes the audio to S3:.

For additional end-to-end Speech AI applications you can build with Amazon Polly, including the voice cloning feature, such as cascaded voice agents and live speech translators, go to the Amazon Polly GitHub repo.

Industry observers note that voice creation takes minutes, so treat it as a provisioning step, not part of a user request. A small workflow (for example, AWS Step Functions or a job queue) can call CreateVoice, check GetVoice every 30 seconds until the voice is active, and then store the voice ID in your configuration. CreateVoice and DeleteVoice share a limit of 1 request per second, so queue bulk creations and deletions.

Recent findings suggest that describeVoices lists your cloned voices alongside the voices built into Amazon Polly. Cloned voices have Origin set to customer. Store the voice ID, Region, language, consent reference, and owner for each voice, and give each voice a unique Name. If a CreateVoice call times out or returns a server error, the voice might already exist, and the SDK’s automatic retries can create a second one. Check DescribeVoices for that name before you try again.

Sources indicate that createVoice returns ThrottlingException when you exceed the 1-request-per-second limit it shares with DeleteVoice, and ServiceQuotaExceededException when the account has reached its cloned-voice quota in that Region. Synthesizing with, or deleting, a voice that is still being created returns ConflictException. If a voice uses your own KMS key, callers without access to the key get an access-denied error. When creation fails, StatusReason gives only a general message, so check the recordings against the preceding recording best practices, then delete the failed voice and create a upcoming one.

Industry observers note that cloned voices are IAM resources, so you can give the role that serves traffic permission to synthesize with one voice of choice. If the voice uses your own KMS key, that role also needs access to the key. Keep polly:CreateVoice and polly:DeleteVoice for a separate provisioning role. Here’s an example policy for the serving role:.

With tags, you can write the same rule once for a whole group of voices using aws:ResourceTag conditions. Review your existing policies too: a statement that allows polly:SynthesizeSpeech on all resources ("Resource": "*") also covers every cloned voice in the account.

Each account has an initial quota of 10 cloned voices per Region. To request an increase, contact your account team or AWS Support. A voice exists only in the account and Region where you created it. To serve another Region or account, create the voice again in that Region from the same recordings, and make sure the speaker’s consent covers every copy.

Industry observers note that before a voice goes live, listen to it reading your own content: product names, numbers, addresses, and the longest sentences you have. The same text can come out slightly differently from one request to the next. For fixed prompts such as phone-line greetings, generate the audio once, approve it with the speaker and your brand team, and serve the stored file. If a name or term comes out wrong, spell it differently in the text or use a Speech Synthesis Markup Language (SSML) tag. Phoneme tags work with cloned voices in English, French, Italian, German, and Spanish. See Supported SSML tags.

Voice cloning in Amazon Polly gives your application a voice people recognize: recorded once, with the speaker’s consent, and ready to use through the Amazon Polly APIs. To get started on the console, make sure Voice cloning is enabled for your account, prepare a recording and the required consent, open the Amazon Polly console, and create your first cloned voice. If you are a new customer and would like to enable voice cloning, reach out to your AWS account team or apply for access to get access.

For the developer guide, refer to the Amazon Polly documentation. For pricing, see the Amazon Polly Pricing Page. For additional speech AI use cases you can build with Amazon Polly, including voice cloning, check out the GitHub repo.

We can’t wait to hear what you build.

Thanks to Trevor Wood, Jonas Rohnke, Suyin Wang, Hannah Barrett, Nikie Xiong, Jeff Barr, and Joely Huang for lending us their voices.

Just over a week ago, we released Granite Switch 4.1, showing that our modular Switch architecture lets you configure a language model with specialized, cache-efficient adapters — adding new expertise on a single endpoint.

Sources indicate that granite Switch 4.1.1 is a patch release. The version number means what it means in software: fully backwards compatible with 4.1, no migration, incremental improvements under the hood.

While we are excited about these new features, what is notable is the speed and efficiency with which our teams could release this enhancement. Apart from training the new ASR model and Decision adapter, nothing was recomputed: the base model is untouched. You compose the latest adapters you want and deploy.

According to recent reports, this pattern can power far more than patch releases to an IBM-provided model. We're working on tutorials and an Adapter SDK so developers and third-party providers can build their own adapters — iterate on versions, test features, and ship updates the way you ship software. More soon.

Until then, test out our latest models, and try out the upcoming multilingual and punctuation capabilities powering our Speech-to-Decisions demo.

Agent Recovery Gone Wrong: Measuring Harm Beyond Duplicate Calls

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (282 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31554v1 Announce Type: latest Abstract: Code-executing LLM agents submit blocks of code that matter several API writes. If a block fails after some of its writes have taken effect, the agent rewrites the block and continues. It is unknown how often such a recovery harms the external state when the failure occurs naturally in the code written by the agent. In this paper, we measure it on recorded trajectories of AppWorld agents. In a stratified random sample of 200 candidate episodes across ten models, 145 are partial executions confirmed by the database state. In the sample, 30 of 143 confirmed partial executions with a determinable outcome are followed by a harmful recovery, and its violation remains at the end of the run, which gives a stratification-weighted estimate of 24.6%. Two thirds of the harmful recoveries duplicate an effect, and the rest delete user data or make a wrong first-time write, e.g., an order of a wrong product. A rule that searches for repeated calls finds 75% of duplications but only 41% of all harm. We also examine two sources of operation identity for an idempotency contract. In a small pilot (17 episodes, one local model), identifiers supplied by the model do not detectably reduce harm, because the model concerns a new identifier for the same operation. Identity derived from the call content, evaluated counterfactually on the sample, would have matched every harmful write in 14 to 18 of the 30 harmful recoveries, but in none of those with a wrong first-time write, and it would also have matched writes required by the task in 30 episodes. Based on these results, we outline design requirements for safer agent recovery.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.31539v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: The correctness of actions taken by agents is typically evaluated against known, externally verified ground truth labels, such as whether a proof is correct or whether code compiles and passes unit tests. However, as coding and science agents are entrusted with more end-to-end autonomy -- proposing interventions, running experiments, and deciding what to deploy and investigate next -- whether an agent's actions genuinely improve an outcome must be inferred from noisy, often inconclusive experiments. To evaluate agents in this setting, we define agent quality as a weighted sum of correct decisions along its trajectory, using sequences of $e$-values as statistical evidence regarding correctness in place of ground-truth labels. Our framework accommodates arbitrarily dependent decisions, data-dependent trajectory termination, dynamically generated hypotheses, and quality measures defined after the trajectory concludes. We construct upper and lower bound estimators and confidence sets for agent quality with statistical guarantees that hold uniformly over agent trajectory distributions and establish instance-wise sharpness of our estimator class. We demonstrate our methods with a case study comparing the success of Claude Opus and Claude Haiku in improving the runtime of an open-source Python package.

Expert-reviewed finance benchmarks rely on fixed, per-item rubrics, which are costly to extend and cannot encode each institution's own standard. In FinAutoRubric, experts specify reusable evaluation guidance, while agents and code carry out query-specific rubric generation, review, and validation. 💡 Key Takeaways
  • When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step.
  • We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license.
  • Industry observers note that with this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

When building an AI agent, selecting a model is only the first step. The agent still needs tools, instructions for finishing the job, a way to manage context growth in long sessions, and guardrails before it executes any consequential actions, like issuing a refund.

We are upgrading Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness to use Strands harness, our open-source agent harness, released earlier this year, available under an Apache 2.0 license. AgentCore harness also introduces lifecycle hooks, so you can apply your own deterministic checks and notifications at defined points in the agent loop.

Industry observers note that with this upgrade, agents that rely on the managed defaults get a recommended model, a task-oriented system prompt, automatic prompt caching (initially for Anthropic models on Amazon Bedrock), and proactive context management. They also get additional built-in tools for planning, web retrieval, filesystem access, context offloading, and task delegation. This gives agents greater capabilities during long tasks, allowing them to keep track of subtasks, reduce context window usage, and delegate work. With hooks, you can transform non-deterministic AI behavior into predictable, safe, and governed workflows by running deterministic code at specific lifecycle checkpoints.

It has been revealed that there’s no upcoming resource type or integration to adopt. You automatically get both updates in the AgentCore harness you already use.

According to recent reports, strands harness provides an assembled agent foundation with recommended instructions, tools, and context management. Amazon Bedrock AgentCore harness operates that foundation as a managed AWS service. The result is a production-grade default agent that doesn’t require you to assemble and operate the harness or its infrastructure yourself.

You do not need to provision compute, bundle and host the agent loop, manage session scaling, or operate tool-execution infrastructure. Each session runs in a secure, kernel-isolated microVM in AgentCore runtime, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with managed compute, scaling, and high availability.

AgentCore achieves this by connecting the harness to the services required for production agents, including session persistence, streaming responses, usage metadata, observability, AgentCore memory, Identity, Gateway, Browser, Code Interpreter, and customer-provided containers. You retain control over the model, instructions, tools, permissions, and lifecycle policies while AgentCore manages the underlying execution environment.

Harness now provides a stronger experience when you use its managed defaults:.

Customer-provided Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, AgentCore Gateway (a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore), Browser, Code Interpreter, inline functions, skills, memory, and customer-provided containers continue to work through the existing harness interfaces.

Harness manages its defaults so that agents using them receive the current AgentCore recommended experience as models, instructions, context management, and built-in capabilities improve.

Explicit configuration always takes precedence:.

When allowedTools is omitted or set to ["*"], Harness provides the current recommended built-in tool set. Because this set can gain capabilities over time, applications with a fixed security or capability boundary should list only the tools they need.

For example, the following configuration permits read-only filesystem access and web retrieval without granting shell access or file modification:.

With lifecycle hooks, you can run your own deterministic code at defined points in the agent loop. For example, an AWS Lambda function can allow or deny a request or a tool call, and an Amazon Simple Notification Service (Amazon SNS) topic or Amazon EventBridge event bus can receive a notification to record activity or start an asynchronous workflow.

Harness supports four lifecycle events:.

In a recent development, only Lambda hooks can change the agent loop. They run synchronously and return allow or deny, with an optional reason. SNS and Amazon EventBridge hooks are notifications and don’t block the agent loop.

Sources indicate that for example, a customer-support agent can investigate an order on its own while a before_tool_call hook checks each refund against an approval limit before the refund tool runs. The following configuration attaches that Lambda function to the harness:.

The function receives the proposed tool call in the hook payload and returns a decision:.

Sources indicate that when the function denies the call, the harness skips the refund and the agent continues, so it can tell the customer that the request was escalated. Each decision also appears in the InvokeHarness response stream as a hookEvent:.

According to recent reports, hooks also apply to subagents. When the agent delegates a task, each tool call the subagent makes runs through the same beforeToolCall and afterToolCall hooks, so delegation can’t bypass your refund policy. The invocation-level hooks (beforeInvocation, afterInvocation) run once for the whole invocation.

You configure hooks with CreateHarness or UpdateHarness. If a Lambda function times out or returns an error, the hook applies its failureMode, which defaults to deny. For timeouts, payload fields, and context limits, see Lifecycle hooks in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Developer Guide.

To see every event and target type working together, try the Refund Desk sample in the Amazon Bedrock AgentCore samples repository on GitHub. A six-step guided tour highlights all four lifecycle events and the AWS Lambda, Amazon SNS, and Amazon EventBridge targets. It also shows validation of client-supplied inline function results and the difference between failureMode deny and allow.

Creating a harness takes a single command. You name it and set up the instructions, context policy, and limits you want. This example creates a Research Coordinator: a harness with a task-oriented system prompt and summarization-based truncation. In a single invocation, it runs a researcher, a synthesizer, and a reviewer as subagents and returns one consolidated report. You get multi-agent orchestration and context management without provisioning infrastructure or wiring the delegation yourself.

According to recent reports, the agentcore harness commands call the harness APIs directly, so you don’t need a CLI project or a deployment step. Install the AgentCore CLI, a capability of Amazon Bedrock AgentCore, with npm:.

According to recent reports, the CLI uses your default AWS credentials. It has no --profile flag, so set the AWS_PROFILE environment variable if you want a specific profile. Save the coordinator’s instructions from the sample as system_prompt.md in your working directory.

Sources indicate that this command passes the coordinator’s system prompt, a summarization policy that keeps the 30 most recent messages intact as the conversation grows, and limits high enough for the full workflow. Because it omits the model, memory, and execution role, the harness uses the current AgentCore recommended model and managed memory, and the CLI creates an execution role in IAM for you.

Creation is asynchronous. Wait for creation to finish. The last command should print READY:.

It has been revealed that invoke your harness with a new session ID. Start with a basic question. The coordinator answers it directly, without calling its subagents:.

Sources indicate that then ask for a full research report in the same session. The coordinator intends the work and delegates to the researcher, synthesizer, and reviewer in order. It runs at most one revision cycle if the reviewer asks for it, and delivers the final report. Reusing the session ID continues the conversation in the same environment.

With --prompt, the CLI prints the completed transcript as JSON when the turn finishes. The research run takes about 10 to 15 minutes. To follow along as it works, leave out --prompt, and the CLI opens an interactive chat.

The same example in Python (boto3), including the full system prompt, is available in the AgentCore samples repository on GitHub.

Recent findings suggest that delete the harness when you’re done. This also deletes its managed memory unless you pass --delete-managed-memory false. The execution role that the CLI created stays in your account, so delete it in the IAM console if you no longer need it.

According to recent reports, on November 11, AgentCore harness began rolling out the Strands harness-backed experience to new and existing harnesses. No customer action is required.

According to recent reports, configuration you explicitly provide remains unchanged. Harnesses that omit the model, system prompt, or truncation configuration, or use allowedTools: ["*"], receive the upgraded managed defaults.

If your application requires fixed behavior or a fixed capability boundary, configure those settings explicitly.

Industry observers note that create and invoke an AgentCore harness as you do today. Use the managed defaults for the complete current recommended experience, or configure individual settings when your application requires fixed behavior.

We look forward to seeing what you build with the upgraded AgentCore harness.

Tech Report: Transformers Model Integration Contracts

📅 03 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1303 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5.
  • In a recent development, when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them.
  • In a recent development, transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

On July 30, 2026, Transformers enabled PyTorch's scaled dot-product attention (SDPA) for T5. As a side effect, UMT5's decoder could attend to future tokens. During training, it could peek at the answer it was supposed to predict. Nothing crashed, and the bug stayed in main for almost two months.

In a recent development, when we later replayed those commits, a small UMT5 model running on CPU flagged it on every one of them. This post is about that model and the tests built around it.

In a recent development, transformers supports over 750 model types, and its test suite is big: 88,000+ CPU tests on main, plus 200,000+ GPU tests in a daily run. Model tests are only part of it: we also test pipelines, training, distributed execution, quantization and attention kernels.

The integration tests load real checkpoints and exercise the model's API on real hardware. Running all of that on every PR would mean keeping a lot of GPUs busy all day long, which isn't practical. By the time a scheduled run finds a regression, it may already be in main.

In a recent development, our approach is to shrink the model instead. We build a fixture: a small model made from the real checkpoint's configuration, with fewer and narrower layers but every kind of layer it has, and its tokenizer and processor files unchanged. It is published once, then reused. We run "fast integration tests" against it on a cheap CPU runner. In our CPU study, the experimental UMT5 fixture used 66 MB of weights; the source checkpoint is 1,227 MB.

This also covers very large models: some don't fit on our standard GPU runners, but their fixtures run on CPU.

Recent findings suggest that model integrators already build tiny test models (Transformers' tiny-random-* checkpoints). We wanted a common recipe, and checks that go beyond loading the model and running a forward pass. The UMT5 bug would have passed a forward pass just fine.

Fixtures won't replace full integration tests, but on PRs they give us a chance to catch bugs before they reach main.

Recent findings suggest that transformers-mic is a proposed standard for packaging these tests. A Model Integration Contract (MIC) has three parts:.

The contract holds if running the usage path on the fixture still produces the baselines.

A contract covers an architecture and a usage path, not a single checkpoint: compatible checkpoints can share a fixture, while each keeps its own expected results. We publish them in huggingface-mic.

For example, the SmolLM contract generates from prompts such as "The capital of France is" and compares its token IDs with a recorded answer. After loading the model and tokenizer, the generation code is, simplified to one prompt:.

According to recent reports, it also compares training loss, checks that gradients are finite and verifies that an optimizer step changes the weights. See the full usage.md.

Sources indicate that A fleet dataset on the Hub pins each MIC to a frozen revision, along with the package versions used to record its baselines. Each CI run records the fleet revision it used, so we can reproduce it later.

On a PR, we pick MICs based on the files the patch changes.

We replayed frozen MICs over five months of Transformers commits. The small UMT5 fixture flagged the regression from its introduction on July 30, 2026 until its fix on September 28. Label log-probabilities differed from the reviewed baseline by 1.22 and training loss by about 0.20.

Sources indicate that one detail mattered: the contract used SDPA, the default attention path. Running only the eager attention variant missed the bug. A fixture only helps if it goes through the same code as the real checkpoint.

We then reverted the fix on a proof branch in Transformers' CI. The check failed with the same differences, and the selected T5 contract's runner step took 13.4 seconds on CPU, excluding setup.

The replay results and the CI demo have the measurements and reproduction details.

The first recipe was simple: make the dimensions smaller and keep fewer layers. That wasn't enough for mixed architectures. Keeping two layers is no use if both use sliding attention and the full-attention layers disappear.

In a recent development, we also keep the original weights file format. Otherwise we would skip the conversion code that runs when a user loads the real checkpoint. The full recipe has more detail.

It has been revealed that the Llama 4 Scout shrink report reveals what this looks like on a big model. 108.6 billion parameters become 44.7 million. The vision stack goes from 34 layers to 2 and the language stack from 48 to 4, keeping the checked layer kinds and MoE routing style.

It has been revealed that our CLI, tmic, creates the contract and builds the fixture. For a newly introduced model, an LLM drafts the usage code and manifest, and CPU and GPU runs measure the candidate baselines. The LLM drafts; it doesn't approve. Changed expectations require human review.

To try it on your machine, use your source checkpoint in place of org/model:.

According to recent reports, it drafts the contract, builds the fixture and records its baselines on your machine, asking you to review each step, and stops before uploading anything. For a upcoming model, the draft comes from an LLM through Inference Providers, billed to your own account (--bill-to ''). The CLI docs cover the individual steps.

Sources indicate that we used agents to build MICs across model families. When they hit an edge case, we fixed the recipe itself rather than the one fixture, with help from model experts. The published models and remaining gaps are in the coverage space.

Industry observers note that with random weights, our Whisper fixture barely responded to changes in the audio. It ran, but that made it a poor test of the audio path.

So we trained it on a few tones paired with words such as "red" and "green". We weren't teaching it speech recognition, just making audio changes visible in its outputs. In our weight-initialization study, the random Whisper fixtures caught 18 of 24 injected faults. The overfit fixtures caught all 24.

That gives us two ways to build the weights:.

The Whisper result doesn't settle which is better. Those were synthetic faults, and we haven't found a real regression caught only by the overfit version. Both versions missed an assisted-decoding bug that the real Whisper checkpoint exposed.

So we keep random weights when they pass the checks, and overfit when we need better sensitivity or readable answers. Training takes seconds, but it is one more step that can fail to converge, and one more thing to maintain. The comparison has the results for both.

As of November 1, 2026, the MIC job in Transformers CI reports failures without blocking PRs. Whether it should block depends on things we haven't measured yet:.

We also don't know how many bugs, like the Whisper assisted-decoding one, only show up with real weights, or whether overfitting catches real bugs that random weights miss.

According to recent reports, coverage is still partial, across model families and the APIs people use. When a regression slips through, we can add the missing usage path and replay it on the broken and fixed versions. We'll keep existing tests until their coverage is accounted for.

Finally, we'd like to link original Hub model pages to their MICs, so a developer or an agent using a checkpoint could start from an example tested on that checkpoint, its environment and its expected outputs.

In a recent development, want to help? Pick an uncovered model from the coverage space, try the tmic workflow, and contribute a usage path or review a generated contract.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (257 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish

arXiv:2605.24514v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Return panels, covariances, and large feature matrices evolve one observation or entry at a time, yet downstream models require an up-to-date low-rank factorization $A_t \approx U_t \Sigma_t V_t^\top$ on every tick - a regime where a full singular value decomposition (SVD) is prohibitive and existing alternatives sacrifice singular vectors, singular values, or long-horizon stability. We present a metric-driven study of Brand-style incremental SVD, built around a unified engine that handles row appends, column appends, rank-1 entry updates, and metrics tracking. For rank-1 entry updates, we derive an explicit projection-based rule $U'\Sigma'(V')^\top = P_U(\widehat{A} + \delta\,e_ie_j^\top)P_V$ that keeps rank fixed while discarding only the out-of-subspace remainder quantifiably, turning Brand's rank-suppression heuristic into an operational scheme. Each patch discards a part whose norm is available at negligible cost; the error at the last refresh plus the sum of these norms since then is an a posteriori error bound $\beta_t$. We then treat refresh scheduling as a first-class design axis, comparing periodic refresh with a bound-triggered rule that refreshes once $\beta_t/\|A_t\|_F$ exceeds a tolerance. The engine tracks error ratios, principal angles, explained variance, and per-update runtime on long synthetic streams and a factor model of exchange-traded funds for covariance and portfolio-risk estimation. With a sensible rank and refresh cadence, incremental SVD matches full-SVD accuracy within a few percent at a fraction of the cost. The bound-triggered rule keeps the relative error below any tolerance above its rank-$k$ optimum, with accuracy close to periodic refresh at a matched number of full SVDs.

arXiv:2611.31522v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: GUI agents can choose correct actions yet fail as interfaces change during deliberation. Latency alone cannot explain these failures because actions may become invalid at different interaction stages. We model four events: environment change, observation availability, decision commitment, and action receipt (EODA). We introduce ChronotopeGym to study these failures under Paused, Replay, and Live execution. Across five tasks, agents can fail in Live despite succeeding when responses remain valid, even when actions meet deadlines. On Moving Balloon, updating a pending click raises success from 0% to 100% without changing response time. Our accelerator-resident GUI controller, Chronotope, maintains compact interaction history and selectively keeps, updates, or redecides pending actions. Compared with Agent S3, Chronotope reduces median end-to-end latency by 85.5% for a 27B model, expanding its performance envelope to 100% Live success at an 8-second deadline versus 0%. Chronotope enables real-time GUI control through compact interaction history, knowing when to preserve, revise, or replace actions, and an overall efficient architectural design that obviates verbose reflection, reasoning, and grounding calls.

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2611.30843v3 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Rotationally invariant estimators clean the eigenvalues of an empirical correlation matrix but keep its noisy eigenvectors. We study an estimator that corrects the eigenvectors by using external information, namely a partition of the assets into groups such as asset classes or regions. The Maximum Variance (MaxVar) estimator restricts the leading eigenvectors to linear combinations of the maximum-variance portfolios of the groups and replaces the rest of the spectrum by a single eigenvalue. It is a factor model with about n parameters instead of n2/2, and it is positive de nite even when the number of observations is smaller than the number of assets n. We apply it to the correlation matrix of 47 futures on stock indices, bonds and currencies, with the three asset classes as groups. In an illustrative Monte Carlo test, in which the reference matrix has the structure assumed by the estimator, the distance to the reference is reduced by one third with respect to the empirical matrix, against less than 10% for the rotationally invariant estimator. The decisive test is the performance of a portfolio on real data: over 1993-2018, the Sharpe ratio of the risk parity portfolio, which involves the inverse of the matrix, is 1.28 with the MaxVar estimator, 1.24 with the rotationally invariant estimator and 1.17 with the empirical matrix, and the advantage increases when the estimation window is shortened.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that CWE-bench is designed to test the limits of frontier cyber capabilities. In our continued pursuit to push the horizon at Collinear AI, CWE-bench v2 opens up a public set of 100 tasks that anyone can run and evaluate their models on. The setup is the same as before. An agent gets a checkout of a real open-source repository and a short instruction, with the goal of finding and fixing a security weakness without breaking existing functionality. Scoring is fully programmatic, so results are deterministic and anyone can reproduce them without extra cost. All our programmatic checks have been curated with the help of LLM judge panels that shape them towards the direction of hardness and fairness. We also maintain a held-out set, so that we can keep tracking progress on tasks no model has seen. To evaluate your model on the held-out set, contact cyber@collinear.ai.

Industry observers note that our goal is to be exhaustive. A defender has to anticipate the ways an attacker could get in, and get it right every single time. These 100 tasks cover 91 different CWEs, spanning a wide range of vulnerability classes. A model that does well here has to understand the multiple weakness surfaces that a potential attacker can exploit. Recognising a familiar pattern is not enough.

As part of our meticulous effort to keep improving quality, for every task we checked that the following questions were true:.

Every task was also reviewed by hand. Open-sourcing the set is part of the same effort to improve quality. We welcome feedback on any task, and contributions to the public set.

It has been revealed that results are tracked in two places on the Hub. The leaderboard on the CWE-bench dataset page covers open-weight models and updates on its own: labs and the community add a result by opening a PR on the model's repo with a results file (how). For the full comparison, including API-only models such as Gemini, Claude and GPT, see the CWE-bench leaderboard Space, where newly introduced models are added through a PR on the Space.

Open-weight models, from the dataset page:.

All evaluated models, including API-only ones:.

Industry observers note that of the 11 models evaluated, Gemini 4 Argon leads with 67.8% pass@1 and 81.0% pass@4, just ahead of Claude Opus 5.5 (67.3% pass@1, 78.0% pass@4). 95 tasks are solved by at least one model, an indication that the tasks are indeed solvable. However, even the leader fails 19% of the set on every attempt, so the long tail is far from solved. The public set, the grader and the harness are open. Run your model, and tell us where it stands.

On cost, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash (1017), Claude Opus 5.5 and Gemini 4 Argon form the Pareto frontier: DeepSeek reaches 57.0% pass@1 at $0.04 per rollout, Opus adds ten points at $1.83, and Gemini edges ahead at $3.92.

It has been revealed that every task is a self-contained Harbor task (a Dockerized environment, an instruction, and a deterministic verifier), and the dataset ships a registry.json. Harbor can therefore run the whole benchmark straight from the Hugging Face repo, without cloning anything yourself:.

In a recent development, -k 4 runs 4 attempts per task, and the reported score is the mean reward over all 400 trials. The dataset is gated: accept its access conditions on the dataset page first. Harbor fetches the tasks with git, so also save your HF token to git's credential helper once:.

The tasks are also tagged rl-environment: the same environments and verifiers can provide rewards for training defensive agents, not just for evaluating them.

arXiv:2611.31521v1 Announce Type: fresh Abstract: Agents that search patient charts must classify claims from retrieved records, including cases with missing or conflicting evidence. In Fast Healthcare Interoperability Resources (FHIR), status fields can change how those records should be interpreted. PatientFlowSynth provides 18,000 tasks from 225 synthetic patients and 18 templates that hold the patient, question, and retrieval program fixed across chart variants representing four evidence states. Re-executing the program verifies each variant's reference answer, evidence sets, and search requirements. Strict success requires a completed response with correct labels and citations exactly matching an accepted evidence set retrieved during the episode. Where required, a tool response must also show a complete search at the specified scope. In a study using GPT-5.6 Luna and 225 synthetic patients (3,600 matched pairs), explicit Encounter-status guidance increased strict success from 40.7% to 51.3% (+10.6 percentage points; 95% patient-bootstrap confidence interval, 8.4 to 12.8). Among cases whose primary reference label was insufficient evidence, label agreement fell from 49.2% to 29.3%. A prespecified two-model replication reproduced both changes. Failed retrieval can mask interpretation errors by producing a correct insufficient-evidence label without examining the relevant records. Additional model comparisons revealed that the benefit of guidance was model-dependent. Retrieval, citation, and classification should be evaluated separately.
