#10166. Announcing Amazon Textract Insights: Verifiable generative AI for documents

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1472 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

Announcing Amazon Textract Insights: Verifiable generative AI for documents

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1472 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing.
  • Today, we are announcing the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights, a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract.
  • Many of the high-value document workloads involve diverse, mixed packets rather than clean, single-purpose files.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Organizations across financial services, insurance, healthcare, and the public sector depend on document processing. They turn scanned files and paper forms into structured data their systems can act on. As generative AI has matured, these organizations want more than accurate text extraction. They want to describe the information they need in their own words and get dependable, auditable answers from complex documents.

Today, we are announcing the general availability of Amazon Textract Insights, a new generative AI feature of Amazon Textract available through a new API within Amazon Textract. With Amazon Textract Insights, you describe the fields you want in natural language and submit a document or a mixed, multi-document packet. You receive structured results in which each value carries a confidence score and page-level grounding, with no model training required.

Many of the high-value document workloads involve diverse, mixed packets rather than clean, single-purpose files. A mortgage file, for example, typically arrives as a single scan holding a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a page of handwritten notes. Each has its own layout and appears in no fixed order. Claims files and onboarding packages can look very similar: typed forms, dense tables, scanned receipts, and free-text letters interleaved in one file.

Recent findings suggest that teams usually take one of two approaches, and each has trade-offs. The first is a custom pipeline that combines optical character recognition, document splitting, classification, a foundation model prompt, and a review step. The team must integrate, scale, and operate all of it. The second is a general-purpose large language model used by default. It returns fluent answers but does not reliably cite the source page or give a confidence score. Without a traceable source and a calibrated score, it is hard to know which values to accept automatically and which to review. This uncertainty often limits how far teams can automate.

Amazon Textract Insights is built for reliable document processing, bringing this entire workflow into a single asynchronous request on Amazon Textract. Rather than assembling and operating a custom pipeline, your team works through one managed API and moves directly to the data it needs.

With Amazon Textract Insights, you define what to extract in a blueprint. A blueprint is a JSON Schema in which each field carries a natural language description of what to find. Each field also has an inference type that determines whether the value is read verbatim from the page or inferred from the content of the document. You can begin with an AWS public blueprint for a common document type, such as a W-2, Form 1040, Form 1098, a passport, or a birth certificate. You can also author your own blueprint for the documents specific to your business.

For a mixed packet, you add the blueprints for each document type you expect to the same project. You then submit a single file of up to 3,000 pages from your own Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket and enable splitting. Amazon Textract Insights splits the packet into logical sub-documents, matches each one to the blueprint that fits it, extracts the requested fields, and returns a confidence score and grounding for each value.

Recent findings suggest that for example, suppose you receive a mortgage application as a single 26-page PDF that contains a W-2, payslips, bank statements, and a loan officer’s handwritten notes. You create an Amazon Textract Insights project with the AWS public W-2, payslip, and bank statement blueprints, add a custom blueprint for loan officer notes, and enable splitting. You then submit the file from your Amazon S3 bucket with a single StartDocumentInsights call. Amazon Textract Insights splits the file into its individual documents, matches each one to its blueprint, and writes the results to your S3 bucket. Each value includes a confidence score and the page and bounding box it was drawn from.

Recent findings suggest that amazon Textract Insights returns two kinds of fields: The first are explicit fields read directly from the page. The second are inferred fields derived from the document’s content. Both return with a confidence score and with grounding that identifies the page and the coordinates the value was drawn from.

It has been revealed that because each value is traceable to its source, a reviewer or an auditor can confirm any result against the original document. You can extend automation to documents that would previously have gone to manual review, while keeping people in the process wherever judgment is required.

“We evaluated Amazon Textract Insights and are excited about its potential. Our medical bills and forms are received from a wide variety of sources and often have different layouts and formats. As a result, extraction rules developed for one source do not always transfer effectively to another.

Industry observers note that with Amazon Textract Insights, we can describe the fields we need in plain language, and the service identifies and extracts the corresponding data. Each extracted value is returned with a confidence score, allowing our team to focus their review efforts only on the fields where the service has lower confidence. We are also excited to explore the document splitting capabilities, which could help automatically separate multi-document files into individual documents and further streamline our document processing workflow.”.

— Vijay Agrawal, Vice President, Information Systems, Symbeo, A CorVel Company.

According to recent reports, we updated Amazon Textract’s reading engine, Amazon Textract Core, improving accuracy, strengthening the handling of dense tables and handwriting, and expanding language coverage to 40 languages for the DetectDocumentText and AnalyzeDocument APIs. All these benefits are available to Amazon Textract customers today with no changes. Your Amazon Textract APIs remain unchanged.

It has been revealed that amazon Textract Core is now generally available in two additional AWS Regions, Asia Pacific (Tokyo) and Europe (Zurich), bringing in-region processing to a total of 18 AWS Regions. Amazon Textract Insights isn’t yet available in these AWS Regions.

Industry observers note that amazon Textract Insights encrypts projects and blueprints at rest with AWS owned keys. To use your own AWS Key Management Service (AWS KMS) customer managed key, specify it in EncryptionConfiguration when you call CreateProject or CreateBlueprint.

Amazon Textract Insights reads documents from, and writes results to, the Amazon S3 buckets specified in your StartDocumentInsights request. Intermediate job data is encrypted at rest with AWS owned keys. If you specify a customer managed key in the request’s EncryptionConfiguration, Amazon Textract Insights uses it to encrypt the job’s intermediate data. All intermediate data is transient and is deleted when the job completes. Your output bucket’s default encryption applies to the results written to your bucket when the job completes. A project’s key does not apply to its jobs.

If you disable your key or remove Amazon Textract’s access to it, Amazon Textract Insights can no longer use data encrypted under it.

It has been revealed that amazon Textract Insights automatically selects the optimal AWS Region within your geography to process your inference requests. This maximizes available compute resources and model availability, and is designed to deliver a consistent customer experience. All data is transmitted encrypted across Amazon’s secure network. Amazon Textract Insights securely routes your inference requests to available compute resources within the geographic area where the request originated. For example, inference requests originating in the United States are processed within the United States. Amazon Textract Core APIs are unchanged and continue to process requests in the AWS Region you call. For the list of destination AWS Regions, see the Amazon Textract documentation guide.

Getting started with Amazon Textract Insights takes four steps.

Define what you need: Start from an AWS public blueprint or describe your own fields in natural language.

Create a project: Add your blueprints to it.

Submit your documents: Send a single document or a mixed packet from your Amazon S3 bucket with one API call.

Recent findings suggest that review the results: Accept values that meet your confidence threshold and route the rest for review. Tune your threshold on a representative sample of your own documents.

In a recent development, amazon Textract Insights supports PDF, PNG, JPEG, and TIFF inputs and processes documents in English, French, German, Italian, Portuguese, and Spanish. It is priced per page rather than per token, with no minimum commitment. For current rates across Amazon Textract, see the Amazon Textract pricing page.

Industry observers note that intelligent document processing has long forced a choice between how far you can automate and how well you can audit the result. Amazon Textract Insights narrows that trade-off so your team can decide where to automate based on evidence rather than guesswork. Learn more about getting started with Amazon Textract Insights.

Visit the Amazon Textract product page.

Follow the Amazon Textract Developer Guide to author a blueprint or start with an AWS blueprint.

Register for Accelerate intelligent document processing with Amazon Textract session at re:Invent.

#10165. Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (1963 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Hugging Face ↗ Open Full Page

Token Pooling-Aware Training for Multi-Vector Embedding Models

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (1963 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document.
  • Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors.
  • It has been revealed that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Multi-vector embedding models give each query token its own opportunity to find a match in a document. This makes them wonderfully expressive for search, but those document vectors add up swiftly. A corpus with millions of documents can contain hundreds of millions of vectors!

Token pooling makes these representations smaller by merging similar token vectors. The more aggressively I compress them, however, the easier it becomes to lose something useful. Pooling-aware training teaches the encoder to preserve the information that matters when its vectors are merged, helping you retrieve better from the same storage budget.

It has been revealed that in this post, I'll explain how pooling works, train a model for compressed retrieval with Sentence Transformers, and explore the resulting quality and storage tradeoff. With pool_factor=4, my normally trained model retains 94.6% of its unpooled NanoBEIR nDCG@10, with a 4x reduction in document vectors. Token pooling-aware training raises that retention to 97.8% at the same storage budget! Let's see how.

According to recent reports, this post builds on pooling-aware training studied in Stefan Josef's Learn to Pool and LightOn's pooling regularization study, which also explores targeted training and adaptive budgets. Here, I'll focus on understanding the method and putting it to work with a short, reproducible Sentence Transformers example.

Pooling-aware training improves retrieval quality at the same vector budget. Details below.

A single-vector embedding model compresses an entire document into one vector. Multi-vector models such as ColBERT instead keep a collection of contextual token vectors, allowing different parts of a query to match different parts of a document.

For example, a query about a laptop with a long battery life can find evidence about the laptop in one part of a document and battery endurance in another. With MaxSim scoring, each query vector selects its best matching document vector, and those scores are added together:.

MaxSim⁡(Q,D)=∑q∈Qmax⁡d∈Dq⊤d \operatorname{MaxSim}(Q, D) = \sum_{q \in Q} \max_{d \in D} q^\top d MaxSim(Q,D)=q∈Q∑​d∈Dmax​q⊤d.

Even with the 2-bit or 4-bit residual quantization supported by Fast-PLAID, storing hundreds of vectors per document adds up. At 4 bits per residual coordinate, 200 vectors of 128 dimensions require 12.8 KB of quantized residuals per document, or 12.8 GB across a million documents. Pooling each document to 50 vectors reduces that to 3.2 GB, at the same dimensionality and precision.

Sources indicate that the useful observation is that many document vectors can be similar. Several tokens might describe closely related concepts, creating an opportunity to represent them together.

Industry observers note that hierarchicalTokenPooling groups similar token embeddings using Ward hierarchical clustering. Starting with one group per token vector, it repeatedly merges the two groups that cause the smallest increase in how spread out the vectors are within their groups. This spread is measured by the sum of squared distances from each vector to its group's mean, so Ward's method favors compact groups of similar vectors.

Sources indicate that these merges build a hierarchy of progressively larger groups, letting us choose a level of compression that fits our budget. We then represent each group by its mean and normalize the resulting vectors again, ready for MaxSim scoring.

You can make compression proportional to document length:.

According to recent reports, with pool_factor=4, documents retain approximately one quarter of their original vectors, so longer documents can keep proportionally more capacity. By default, the first token is protected from merging and pooling applies only to document embeddings, leaving query embeddings unchanged.

HierarchicalTokenPooling offers three alternative controls:.

This distinction matters when document lengths vary. With pool_factor=4, a longer document can retain approximately one quarter of its vectors, allowing its representation to grow with its content. With distance_threshold, the vector count can grow when more distinct embeddings need to be preserved.

In a recent development, adaptive pooling uses a shared distance threshold to merge similar embeddings more aggressively while preserving more vectors for documents with distinct content. It can be used with any multi-vector model, including one trained without a pooling-aware objective.

Rather than choosing a threshold manually, you can calibrate it for a target average vector count. Given a representative sample of your corpus in calibration_documents:.

Calibration only needs document embeddings and returns a threshold you can reuse when indexing. The target is an average, so individual documents can receive more or fewer than 16 vectors. The achieved average can also change on another corpus.

Pooling can already be useful on an ordinary multi-vector model. The difficulty appears when a document contains a distinction that matters for retrieval, but merging its vectors makes that distinction harder to recover. The original training objective never required the model to work with these compressed representations. But, you can teach it to do exactly that.

Recent findings suggest that if you've used Matryoshka embeddings, the training principle will feel familiar. Matryoshka applies a retrieval objective at several embedding widths, teaching smaller prefixes to remain useful. Pooling-aware training applies the objective to representations with fewer token vectors.

For my example, each training batch contributes two losses:.

L=12Lunpooled+12Lpooled \mathcal{L} = \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{unpooled}} + \tfrac{1}{2}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{pooled}} L=21​Lunpooled​+21​Lpooled​.

The first term teaches the model to retrieve with its full representations. The second teaches it to arrange its token embeddings so that useful matches survive pooling. Both objectives patch the same encoder, giving it feedback about retrieval before and after compression.

Industry observers note that ward clustering makes discrete decisions about which tokens belong together. During training, HierarchicalTokenPooling uses a straight-through estimator to pass gradients from pooled vectors back to their member tokens, without differentiating the cluster assignments. The encoder can then learn from retrieval errors made with its pooled representations.

MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss wraps an existing multi-vector retrieval loss and applies it using your chosen poolers:.

CachedMultiVectorMultipleNegativesRankingLoss supplies the retrieval objective. It teaches each query to score its relevant document above the negative documents in the batch. By default, it uses model.similarity, using the model's similarity setting (MaxSim in this example) and kernel settings. A model configured with similarity_fn_name="meanmaxsim" would also use MeanMaxSim during training.

Gradient caching allows the encoder to process small mini-batches while retaining a larger set of in-batch negatives. My training script uses mini-batches of 64 with a training batch size of 256.

In a recent development, multiVectorTokenPoolingLoss adds the compression objective. Here, None means that one variant uses the original embeddings, while pooling supplies the factor-4 variant. The two weights average their losses. Pooling variants reuse the computed token embeddings, so each additional pooler adds clustering and scoring work without requiring a separate encoder pass for that variant.

Recent findings suggest that the poolers can also be custom BaseTokenPooling implementations that preserve gradients through their input embeddings. You can adapt the training objective to the representation you want to deploy.

Replace the factor-4 pooler with your chosen deployment configuration, or include several poolers and choose weights for their losses.

Recent findings suggest that the complete training script includes the dataset, trainer, validation loss, and small retrieval evaluations during training. From a checkout of the repository, run both variants locally with uv:.

It has been revealed that the script declares its training and kernel dependencies, so uv installs them for you. Compatible kernels are enabled automatically.

This runs the pooling-aware variant on an A10G GPU with a four-hour time limit. Passing HF_TOKEN as a secret lets the script upload the trained model to your Hub account when training finishes. To run the ordinary-loss baseline as well, repeat the command with --baseline after the script URL.

It has been revealed that you can accelerate MaxSim scoring, Ward clustering, and supported backbone operations with kernels. Install the training and kernel dependencies:.

In the training example above, replace the model and pooler initialization before constructing the loss:.

Hierarchical poolers inherit the model's kernel settings by default, so you only need to enable kernels on the model.

Sentence Transformers selects compatible kernels for your setup and uses the existing implementation wherever a replacement isn't available. For example, the default MaxSim kernel scores queries against documents without building the full token similarity matrix in memory, but it does require CUDA and Triton.

It has been revealed that the default Ward clustering kernel considerably speeds up hierarchical clustering by running on CUDA instead of the CPU. We're talking about 30-150x faster than SciPy depending on the setting.

Let's load the pooling-aware model and retrieve with compressed document embeddings. Kernel settings aren't saved with the model, so add use_kernels=True when loading if you'd like to use them for inference too:.

The pooler compresses the document embeddings after the encoder's forward pipeline, reducing the total from 58 vectors to 16 while leaving query embeddings unchanged. Mars still receives the highest similarity score, followed by Jupiter and Venus, so the ranking is preserved despite storing far fewer document vectors.

You can change pool_factor at inference to explore a different storage budget with the same trained model. For repeated use, you can also pass token_pooling=pooling when initializing MultiVectorEncoder to make it the runtime default. The pooler's tasks still control which inputs are compressed (e.g. only documents).

To investigate, I trained two models from answerdotai/ModernBERT-base, each with a fresh 128-dimensional token projection:.

Both runs use one epoch over the same 120,000 MS MARCO triplets, seed 42, and matching initialization and optimization settings. The training token cap is 300, and short queries are expanded to at least 32 token positions to provide additional contextual query vectors. Only the loss differs between the two experiments, and I didn't run a hyperparameter search.

It has been revealed that I evaluated both models on NanoBEIR@13, reporting mean nDCG@10 (%). The figure compares ordinary and pooling-aware training with pool factors of 2, 3, 4, and 6, alongside unpooled retrieval. The table also includes fixed caps and adaptive thresholds, showing how the training benefits transfer to other pooling settings.

For adaptive pooling, I calibrated a separate threshold for each encoder and NanoBEIR corpus, using its unpooled document embeddings to match the average vector counts under caps of 64, 32, and 16. Short documents bring those averages below their respective caps.

At the trained pool_factor=4, nDCG@10 improves from 49.03 to 51.23, while storing 74.8% fewer document vectors than unpooled retrieval. This increases score retention from 94.6% to 97.8%, where retention is the pooled mean nDCG@10 divided by each model's own unpooled mean. Unpooled retrieval also improves, from 51.84 to 52.39.

According to recent reports, the gains extend to fixed caps and adaptive pooling, even though training used only the full representation and proportional pooling. At an average of 29.58 vectors per document, adaptive pooling retains 97.3% of the pooling-aware model's unpooled score while storing 84.7% fewer document vectors. The normally trained model retains 93.3% at the same budget.

If index size is your main concern, I would reach for these options in this order:.

Recent findings suggest that if the model's default dimensionality is larger than 128, I would consider Matryoshka truncation and fine-tuning earlier as well. These approaches can be combined, so evaluate the resulting index size and retrieval quality with your search engine and corpus.

Recent findings suggest that multiVectorMatryoshkaLoss trains token embeddings to remain useful after truncation. You can wrap it with MultiVectorTokenPoolingLoss to train for both smaller dimensions and fewer document vectors, reusing the encoder's embeddings across the compression settings.

Recent findings suggest that try the complete training example, choose a budget that matters for your application, and compare it with a matched ordinary-loss run. The accompanying evaluation script measures unpooled retrieval, caps of 64, 32, 16, 8, and 4 vectors, and pool factors of 2 through 6, so you can plot the quality and storage tradeoff for your own model.

With a few extra lines in the training objective, a smaller document representation becomes something the model actively learns to use. That opens up an exciting amount of room to make multi-vector retrieval more practical!

Stephen Quinn joined the National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) in 2004 and serves as a senior computer scientist in the Information Technology Laboratory (ITL). Mr. Quinn is the lead author for Integrating NIST risk management project work within the paradigm of Enterprise Risk Management (ERM). He is also program manager for the National Checklist Program and the National Online Informative Reference (OLIR) programs at NIST. He is a co-originator of the NIST Security Content Automation Protocol (SCAP).

Recent findings suggest that stephen was named to the “Federal 100” by the trade publication Federal Computer Week (FCW) and received the Department of Commence Gold Medal Award for his work in automating security protocols for applications. Prior to joining NIST, Steve worked in the private sector as a consultant to the Department of Defense and large commercial outsourcings with Wall Street banking firms and insurance companies. Specifically, he comes from an operational background, having owned two companies that provided service offering for vulnerability assessments, designing security architectures, code development, risk management, certifications and accreditations, and ST&Es. His research experience and practitioner experience includes managing and remediating risks specific to computer viruses/malware, intrusion detection systems (IDSs), vulnerability/misconfiguration identification, categorization, and remediation.

Industry observers note that arXiv:2611.34068v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Ad platforms and marketplaces show bidders a bid landscape, the estimated chance of winning at each candidate bid, and increasingly let agents built on reasoning language models choose the bid. We give six open reasoning models of 4B to 14B parameters such landscapes, with win curves from eBay closing prices and from a simulated advertising market (AuctionNet), and score their bids on held-out auctions against an exact calculator. Because the agent is handed the estimates, the lost value can be split by cause. Two failures belong to the models. They pass over the best option even when the values written in their own trace already rank it first, and their wrong answers lean toward the highest bid on the menu. The lean is about the bid's size, not its place in the list, and it survives sampling. At 768 forced tokens on eBay, under pay-your-bid pricing, the wrong answers cost bidders 7-17% of the surplus the calculator's bids earn. Arithmetic errors are rare. Two further losses come from operator choices. A token cap cuts traces short: allowed to stop on their own within 4,096 tokens, five models recover 91-100% of the calculator's lead over a model that does no reasoning. Asking for the answer while the reasoning block is still open misreads it: closing the block first lifts the weakest model from 42% to 84% on eBay and from 24% to 81% on AuctionNet. Finally, an audit that flags bids disagreeing with the trace's own numbers, and overrides them with the calculator's bid, raises the share of the calculator's lead recovered at 768 forced tokens from 42-85% to 84-100% on eBay under nested cross-validation, and the same reader settings transfer from eBay to AuctionNet.

arXiv:2611.31345v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: In recent years, multimodal large language models (MLLMs) have achieved significant progress in chart-to-code generation. However, existing benchmarks mainly focus on static charts, overlooking interactive charts that enable richer and more expressive data exploration. Unlike static chart-to-code generation, which emphasizes visual consistency, interactive chart-to-code evaluation targets behavioral consistency, requiring chart states to evolve correctly under sequences of user interactions, thereby rendering traditional one-step evaluation paradigms ineffective. To address this gap, we introduce ChartInt, the first benchmark specifically designed for interactive chart-to-code generation. ChartInt consists of 2,779 carefully annotated examples covering common interaction patterns such as hover, highlight, and tooltips. Additionally, ChartInt incorporates editing tasks such as data updates, style adjustments, and cross-chart style transfer to expand real-world application scenarios. To enable reliable evaluation of interaction behavior, we propose a preset state snapshot protocol that predefines target interaction states and deterministically triggers interaction events, transforming dynamic behaviors into reproducible evaluation targets. Based on this protocol, we design a multi-dimensional evaluation framework measuring semantic and stylistic consistency. Experiments show that while current MLLMs perform well on static charts, their performance drops significantly on interactive tasks, highlighting the need for interaction-aware benchmarks.

This paper presents the techno-economic optimization of the Soroti Integrated Renewable Energy Microgrid (SIREM), a hybrid renewable system for grid-access expansion where Soroti District household grid access stands at 16.7\%. The microgrid integrates concentrating solar power (CSP) with thermal storage, biogas combined cycle generation, and lithium iron phosphate battery storage. Using Xendee optimization software with six years of NASA POWER data, the optimal configuration comprises a 37 MW CSP field, 70 MWh molten-salt storage, a 5 MW CSP turbine, a 6 MW biogas CCGT, and a 10 MWh battery system. The design delivers 61.3 GWh annually with a 42.91% IRR, 2-year payback, and levelized cost of electricity of 0.1991 USD/kWh generation (0.3752 USD/kWh load-served), achieving 32.2% total savings versus grid-only supply while exporting 28.8 GWh annually, demonstrating the viability of hybrid renewable microgrids for grid expansion in sub-Saharan Africa.

BotPsy: On-Device Personal Assistant with a Sub-Billion-Parameter Agentic Language Model

📅 11 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 11 min read (2164 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~11 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time.
  • Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment.
  • In a recent development, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Frontier cloud LLMs carry high operational costs that can fluctuate unexpectedly, and relying on such third-party models introduces vulnerabilities, as providers can modify, deny, or deprecate access at any time. Furthermore, proprietary models offer limited customization for specific workflows, while posing risks to privacy, data control, and transparency. Besides, not every task demands frontier-level intelligence: small, specialized agents can be equally capable on specific tasks and significantly cheaper to run, since many routine or smaller workloads can be processed efficiently on-device. As intelligence per parameter continues to improve rapidly, we aim to stand at the forefront of this shift toward performant, privacy-focused, self-hosted models.

Tether AI Research introduces BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model introduce BotPsy, a 0.8B-parameter model designed for function calling and agentic workflows, built on top of Qwen3.5-0.8B and suitable for on-device deployment. BotPsy is a "personal assistant" that uses tools to perform a variety of simple tasks for the user, in domains such as web search & research, travel & lifestyle, commerce & finance, business & customer operations, device & vehicle control, files & documents, calendar, and email & messaging. Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty. BotPsy achieves state-of-the-art (SOTA) tool-use and agentic performance for its size, outperforming every model of up to 1.2B parameters that we tested (Figures 1 and 2). Designed for secure on-device workflows, it provides exceptional instruction-following reliability and efficiency while keeping user data private. As a small model, BotPsy still makes mistakes and is not intended for high-stakes use; please read the Intended Use and Limitations for more information.

🤗 Model (safetensors)  |  📦 GGUFs (bf16, Q8, Q4).

In a recent development, building upon the foundation of BotPsy, future development by Tether Data, S.A. de C.V. (“Tether AI Research”, “we”, “our”) will focus on expanding on-device agentic capabilities to seamlessly integrate with an even broader array of hardware and local services. Tether's Hypersearch will evolve to support more robust decentralized peer-to-peer (P2P) queries, further ensuring private, encrypted web searches that bypass corporate trackers. QVAC Fabric local fine-tuning mechanisms will be optimized to adapt more deeply to individual user preferences, workflows, and specialized tool environments. Future iterations will allow the smartphone interface to smoothly delegate heavy computational tasks to home PCs or trusted secure P2P nodes during offline-online transitions. Privacy protocols will be continuously strengthened to guarantee that all personal data, credentials, and decisions remain strictly on local hardware. Collaborative features will be introduced to allow secure agent-to-agent communication across trusted local networks without compromising user confidentiality. Ultimately, these advancements will solidify BotPsy as a fully autonomous, highly capable personal AI ecosystem that keeps consumers entirely in control of their digital lives.

Recent findings suggest that botPsy is based on Qwen3.5-0.8B and is post-trained in four sequential stages: Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT), Multi-teacher On-Policy Distillation (MOPD), and two rounds of Reinforcement Learning (RL). Each stage uses the previous stage's best checkpoint as its starting point and benefits from a different learning signal: imitation of reference trajectories, the token distributions of much larger teacher models, and rule-based tool-calling rewards (see Figure 3).

Our approach uses four stages of training, which learn from three types of signal: demonstrations, specialist teachers, and verifiable rewards.

Learning from demonstrations (SFT).

In a recent development, we first perform full-parameter supervised fine-tuning on tool-use conversations. These include multi-turn agent trajectories from simulated environments, replayed single, parallel and multi-step calls, and cases where no tool should be called.

In a recent development, next, the student is trained with on-policy distillation (OPD): it generates its own responses, and a specialist teacher provides feedback on every token, using the per-token reverse KL divergence as the training signal. To build the teachers, we first RL-trained three Qwen3.5-4B models to specialize in tool use, general reasoning, and instruction following. During training, every prompt is routed to one of these teachers. This stage mainly aims to recover knowledge and instruction following, which degraded during the SFT stage, although the tool-use metrics also increase (see Figure 4).

Learning from rules and environments (RL stages).

Finally, the model is trained with reinforcement learning using DAPO [1], learning only from rewards computed by rules and verifiers. The first round focuses on tool calling, accompanied by instruction following and STEM multiple-choice questions. As in Tool-N1 [2], the tool-calling reward first checks the reasoning and tool-call format. Instead of Tool-N1's binary correctness reward, however, it gives fine-grained partial credit in the spirit of ToolRL [3], matching the predicted tool names, argument names, and argument values against the ground truth.

Recent findings suggest that the second round widens the training mix to general-domain verifiable tasks: math, code, knowledge (multiple-choice) questions, instruction following, structured outputs, and multi-step tool use in a simulated workplace environment. Although this mix contains no multi-turn conversations, it further improves multi-turn function calling.

Recent findings suggest that each stage of training uses a different data mixture (Figure 5). The SFT stage focuses mainly on tool use and prepares the ground for the subsequent stages. The MOPD mixture combines tool-use, knowledge and instruction-following data, both to further improve function calling and to recover the general-domain regressions from the SFT stage. The first RL stage again focuses mainly on tool use, while the second RL stage shifts the balance toward general-domain data (instruction following, knowledge, math and code), keeping a smaller share of tool use.

It has been revealed that botPsy roughly doubles the tool-use performance of its Qwen3.5-0.8B base and is the strongest of the five models on five of the six agentic benchmarks: BFCL v4 (44.0 vs 23.4), ACEBench (58.7 vs 30.1), τ-bench (51.5 vs 23.2), BrowseComp-Plus (4.5 vs 1.9) and ToolSandbox (64.6 vs 30.5). On all five, it is also ahead of Qwen3.5-2B-Think, a model 2.5× its size (37.7, 55.4, 46.5, 2.8 and 41.2 respectively; see Table 1). On Claw-Eval, Qwen3.5-2B-Think leads (48.9 vs 46.5).

Table 1: Tool-use and agentic benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined; multipliers give parameter count relative to BotPsy-0.8B. The average is the unweighted mean of the six benchmarks. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

According to recent reports, tool-use training did not cost general knowledge: GPQA Diamond rises from 33.2 to 38.1 and MMLU-Pro from 41.6 to 48.9, the best of the models at 1.2B parameters or below (LFM2.5-1.2B-Think: 35.0 and 39.4; MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 15.8 and 40.0). Knowledge still scales mainly with parameter count, and Qwen3.5-2B-Think scores well above (59.9 and 65.5). BotPsy is therefore designed to call tools for facts it does not know, not to serve as a knowledge model.

Sources indicate that table 2: General-knowledge benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

BotPsy is the best of the five at following explicit instructions: IFEval 90.8 (base 59.7; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 80.0) and IFBench 55.9 (base 22.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 40.9). On Multi-IF, which tests instruction following over three turns in eight languages, it scores 67.2, on par with Qwen3.5-2B-Think (66.9) and LFM2.5-1.2B-Think (68.2). It starts strongest (84.3 in turn 1, the highest of the five) but drops faster as instructions accumulate (51.0 in turn 3, vs 56.5 and 56.2 for those two models). Lower-resource languages remain a weakness: Hindi (24.5) and Russian (57.6) are far below the 72–80 reached in English, Chinese, French, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese.

According to recent reports, table 3: Instruction-following benchmarks (0–100, higher is better). Best score per row in bold, second best underlined. See Evaluation Footnotes for details of the evaluation setup.

The largest relative gains come in multi-turn, stateful interaction, where BotPsy leads four of the five multi-turn benchmarks (Figure 6). On BFCL v4 multi-turn it rises from 7.5 to 46.1, nearly double Qwen3.5-2B-Think (23.8), and on ACEBench Agent from 7.9 to 28.3 (Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 16.2). On τ²-bench it doubles its base in retail (67.8 vs 33.9, a narrow lead over Qwen3.5-2B-Think at 65.5) and reaches 82.5 in telecom, where the agent has to guide a user through troubleshooting over many turns (MiniCPM5-1B-Think: 74.0; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 69.3). It is also the most reliable of the five at single calls (BFCL non-live: 83.0) and at not calling a tool when none fits (BFCL hallucination: 86.1).

BotPsy's weaker spots are open-ended search and a few areas where Qwen3.5-2B-Think still leads. BotPsy's BrowseComp-Plus score of 4.5 is the best of the five, but low in absolute terms, and on BFCL web search (14.0) and memory (16.3) it trails Qwen3.5-2B-Think (19.8 and 26.1). On Claw-Eval, BotPsy improves clearly on its base (46.5 vs 39.3) but remains slightly below Qwen3.5-2B-Think (48.9). On ACEBench's special cases (incomplete or erroneous requests), Qwen3.5-2B-Think is also ahead (58.0 vs 51.3), although BotPsy is far above its base there (13.7). τ³-banking is the one multi-turn benchmark where BotPsy does not lead: no model gets above 5 (BotPsy 4.1, unchanged from its base; Qwen3.5-2B-Think 4.8).

According to recent reports, botPsy can handle a variety of use cases and scenarios. Figure 7 breaks the benchmark scenarios down by app group, separating simple scenarios (single turn, one tool call) from complex ones (multi-turn or multi-tool). The overall scores quoted in this section are averaged over all scenarios; the bottom row of Figure 7 is an unweighted mean of the seven groups, so its numbers differ.

Simple scenarios score 70–79 in every app group with a meaningful sample (Communication & Social has only 6). Overall, BotPsy scores 75, about 21 points above its base model (54) and slightly above Qwen3.5-2B-Think (70).

On complex scenarios, BotPsy scores 39.5 overall, against 17.9 for its base and 30.8 for Qwen3.5-2B-Think. The gain is largest in Communication & Social (61 vs 13 for the base), Commerce & Services (58 vs 27) and Device & System Management (46 vs 15). Qwen3.5-2B-Think is ahead only in Personal Productivity & Work (64 vs 58, 38 scenarios, mostly Claw-Eval), and MiniCPM5-1B-Think is marginally ahead in Communication & Social (61.5 vs 60.5). Multi-step tasks still score lower than single calls, which remains the main limit for harder tasks.

Complex Information Retrieval & Research scenarios score 15 (single calls: 79). Most are BrowseComp-Plus deep-research questions, which stay hard for every model in this size range (base: 9; Qwen3.5-2B-Think: 14).

In a recent development, botPsy reaches correct answers with much less reasoning than its base, and with fewer turns on multi-turn agent tasks. This aligns with our explicit focus on reasoning efficiency throughout training. All comparisons below are made on the same questions or tasks (those that all five models answered correctly or solved), so differences in difficulty do not drive the numbers. Reasoning tokens are counted with each model's own tokenizer.

It has been revealed that shorter reasoning, with higher accuracy. Compared with its base, BotPsy uses 1.4–3.1× fewer reasoning tokens per correct answer on GPQA Diamond (3,690 vs 11,563), MMLU-Pro (1,912 vs 5,105), IFEval (3,148 vs 4,433) and IFBench (4,204 vs 11,576), while scoring higher on all four (Figure 8). It is not the shortest model everywhere: LFM2.5-1.2B-Think writes shorter reasoning on MMLU-Pro, IFEval and IFBench, and MiniCPM5-1B-Think on IFEval and IFBench, but at lower accuracy than BotPsy on each.

Fewer turns than the base on multi-turn agent tasks. On τ²-bench tasks that all five models solve, BotPsy needs fewer assistant turns than its base (Figure 9):.

Sources indicate that it does this while passing 2.0× (retail) and 2.6× (telecom) as many tasks as the base. MiniCPM5-1B-Think uses fewer turns on retail (8.7), but passes only 9.9% of retail tasks.

BotPsy has been developed to advance the state of the art and to support research and educational uses. Models developed based on our work could be suitable for tasks in domains such as device & system management (settings, files & documents, clocks & alarms), personal productivity & work (calendar & tasks, email, collaboration tools), communication (messaging), information retrieval & research (web search, weather, news), media & lifestyle (video, music, recipes & fitness, photos) and commerce & services (maps & travel, finance, shopping & delivery). Due to its small parameter count, it is best suited to tasks of low to medium difficulty.

BotPsy has been primarily trained and tested in English, which is the recommended language. It has also been evaluated on Multi-IF, which covers seven additional languages (Chinese, French, Hindi, Italian, Portuguese, Russian and Spanish): it performs well in most of them, but scores much lower in Hindi and Russian. BotPsy is a small language model, and it makes mistakes. It is not intended for safety-critical or high-stakes automated decisions, or for applications involving money, personal information, health and other sensitive topics.

#10157. How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 10m • 📚 Deep Dive (2007 w)
📖 Baca
AI & Tech ⚠️ Warning 🌐 Amazon ↗ Open Full Page

How Standard Bank Group automates AI risk assessment for generative AI

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 10 min read (2007 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Amazon

⏱️ ~10 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group.
  • Industry observers note that having an AI policy is one thing.
  • Standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

This post is co-written with Tala Qraitem from AWS and Jörg Fischer from Standard Bank Group.

Industry observers note that having an AI policy is one thing. Proving, one use case at a time, that AI systems follow it is another. Every new generative AI application adds one more system to prove. Teams can now build one in days, but each still needs a risk committee’s approval before it reaches customers or employees. When that approval depends on reviewers reading documents and testing the system by hand, governance becomes the slowest step in the pipeline.

Standard Bank Group chose to automate that proof. Working with AWS Professional Services, the bank deployed an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own policies. The assessment produces reports and a dashboard that show what is already in place, what is working well, and what still needs mitigation. This post explains how the assessment runs on AWS and what Standard Bank Group learned from its first runs.

According to recent reports, standard Bank Group didn’t need a new AI policy. Like most large banks, it already had an established model risk practice that covers concerns such as explainability and fairness, and a change risk process that assesses each new use case according to its level of risk before it goes live.

Generative AI increases the complexity, because models and tooling change every three to six months, yet each use case still needs to meet the same high security and compliance bar.

“At Standard Bank, this assessment demonstrates how we are working with AWS to embed intelligent, automated risk management into our AI journey, allowing us to accelerate meaningful business value while maintaining the trust and controls that banking demands. We believe responsible AI is not about slowing innovation down but enabling it to build and scale with confidence.”.

— Jörg Fischer, Group Chief Information and AI Officer, Standard Bank Group.

The goal was to automate evidence gathering and testing, then feed the results into the approval gates Standard Bank Group already runs. Review and approval stay with the risk committee, but the committee now bases each decision on consistent evidence, collected the same way across use cases.

Figure 1 shows how the assessment’s components fit together in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting.

Figure 1: The assessment pipeline in Standard Bank Group’s AWS account, from intake through evaluation to reporting.

Industry observers note that the assessment runs entirely in Standard Bank Group’s own AWS account. Documents, code, and test results stay in an Amazon Simple Storage Service (Amazon S3) bucket there. The AWS Well-Architected Tool handles intake, AWS Step Functions orchestrates the pipeline, and a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock evaluates the evidence. It uses a technique called LLM-as-a-judge, in which a large language model checks evidence against defined criteria.

With Amazon Bedrock, Standard Bank Group could use a foundation model without stepping outside the controls it already runs on AWS. The bank controls access to the model through AWS Identity and Access Management (IAM), just as it does for its other AWS workloads. Amazon Bedrock doesn’t share the bank’s prompts or model outputs with model providers, and doesn’t use them to train models. Because Amazon Bedrock offers many foundation models through one API, the team can move to a newer judge model by changing a configuration setting instead of rebuilding the pipeline.

Each assessment moves through four steps. In the first two, a pre-assessment agent collects evidence about the use case, then the pipeline examines it and tests the application directly. The third evaluates that evidence against controls. The fourth summarizes the results in a standard, predefined format and delivers them to the people who act on them.

The custom lens in the Well-Architected Tool holds about 40 questions, each covering a risk event such as incomplete technical documentation or insufficient human oversight. Delivery teams no longer fill it in from scratch. A pre-assessment agent running on AWS Fargate scans the use case’s code repository and documentation. It maps relevant files to each question and pre-populates the lens with answers and links to the evidence. The delivery team then reviews those answers, corrects any mistakes, and adds the evidence the agent couldn’t find.

The pipeline works from four kinds of evidence.

Recent findings suggest that for documents and code, the pipeline checks whether each artifact contains what its mapped control requires. Each control comes from an international AI standard or framework, or from Standard Bank Group’s own policies. An incident procedure, for example, needs to describe how incidents are reported.

It has been revealed that for live testing, the pipeline calls the application through its AWS Lambda function or API. The delivery team supplies questions a typical user would ask. The pipeline adds a built-in set of jailbreak attempts and off-topic questions, which the application is expected to decline. It also sends the same prompt several times, in its original and reworded forms, and uses an embedding model on Amazon Bedrock to check that the answers stay consistent in meaning. Where the team provides expected answers, the pipeline measures how closely the responses match them. Every response is stored in Amazon S3, so reviewers can see exactly what the application generated.

In this step, a foundation model on Amazon Bedrock acts as the judge. The assessment uses the model as-is with no fine-tuning or customization. (Model availability varies by AWS Region, so check the supported models by Region before you deploy.) For each question, the model checks whether specific evidence appears in the artifacts and in the application’s responses, and returns yes or no.

Every check maps to a control in an international standard or framework for AI management, AI risk, or AI security. Standard Bank Group also customized the lens with judge questions built from its own standards, bringing the total to more than 300. The checks cover the eight AWS responsible AI dimensions in the following table:.

Each risk receives a likelihood score, the share of required evidence the model couldn’t find, and a fixed severity level that the bank’s risk team can adjust. Together they produce a rating from Very low to Critical. Each missing piece of evidence maps to a specific mitigation and to the clause of the standard or policy it came from. A risk officer can then trace any findings back to their source when explaining decisions to a regulator. Figure 2 follows one missing piece of evidence through this process, from the evidence request to the recommended fix.

Figure 2: How one finding is traced from evidence to fix.

Standard Bank Group protects and checks the assessment’s output in two ways. Every AI model interaction is protected by Amazon Bedrock Guardrails, ensuring alignment with the bank’s established security and responsible AI standards. The assessment’s model calls pass through the same safeguards the bank enforces across its AWS accounts for its AI workloads. These guardrails screen for harmful content and for attempts to manipulate the model.

According to recent reports, the assessment is also designed so its output can be checked. Instead of asking the model for an open-ended opinion, the pipeline asks narrow yes-or-no questions, each worded to match a specific control. A fixed formula that the risk team can inspect turns those answers into scores. Each evaluation runs multiple times to measure how consistent the answers are and any inconsistent findings are flagged in the review interface. Every judgment is stored with the evidence behind it so that reviewers and auditors can trace how it was reached.

The pipeline summarizes the results in a standard format and delivers them as an executive presentation, a mitigation checklist, a detailed technical report, and an Amazon CloudWatch dashboard that tracks scores across use cases over time. Before a gate decision, reviewers confirm findings in a custom review interface with single sign-on. There they can add the use case, review the questions, amend answers with a business justification, and rewrite the output.

The assessment produces evidence against controls. It doesn’t certify compliance with any regulation, and Standard Bank Group remains responsible for its own regulatory determinations.

International standards give every use case a common baseline, but the bank’s risk committees approve use cases against its own policy. A question factory addresses this by generating extra judge questions from internal documents. Standard Bank Group’s risk team used it to turn internal policies into checks that run on every use case.

Sources indicate that because those checks are derived directly from policy language, a policy change becomes a test change. Every subsequent assessment applies the updated rule automatically, with minimal manual rework by the risk team.

“Most organizations treat policy as something you read. Standard Bank Group treats it as something you run. When every rule becomes a check that runs against the live system, a policy update stops being a memo and becomes a test. That fundamentally changes how fast a bank can scale AI responsibly.”.

— Sri Elaprolu, Director, Frontier AI Science & Engineering, AWS.

In a recent development, the assessment fits into three stages of the use case lifecycle. During a proof of concept, it is optional, giving teams an early view of potential gaps. At the build stage, it becomes mandatory, and the approval gate draws on its results as formal evidence. Today the assessment runs in Standard Bank Group’s production environment, evaluating use cases before they go live. After live workloads are connected, the assessment will rerun on a schedule or whenever code or configuration changes, keeping the evidence current well beyond launch. The bank’s teams already trigger assessments on their own through a central system where use cases flow from intake to evaluation in a single workflow.

Industry observers note that at Standard Bank Group, the assessment reduced a traditionally manual two-week review to a comprehensive risk report generated in approximately two hours, demonstrated across six assessments. It also delivered a 14% improvement in use-case risk scores after remediation. This strengthens responsible AI governance, reduces compliance bottlenecks, and shortens the path from assessment to production.

This approach can benefit three groups involved in approving AI use cases:.

Sources indicate that “Adoption of AI at scale across the enterprise requires trust, both internally and with our customers. This assessment is proving key in enabling all our product teams to demonstrate that they are building enterprise-grade solutions aligned with both our own and industry best practices.”.

— Duncan Macdonald, Chief Technology Officer, Standard Bank Group.

Banks designed approval gates for systems that changed a few times a year. Generative AI applications change with every prompt update, model version, and new data source. As they take on more autonomous tasks, the number of decisions that need evidence keeps growing. Adding reviewers can’t keep pace with that rate of change.

Recent findings suggest that standard Bank Group’s approach points to a different operating model. When policies become tests and evidence is collected automatically, governance moves out of a checkpoint at the end of delivery and into the system itself. Every AI application in the portfolio can carry a current, auditable record of how it meets the bank’s standards, refreshed whenever its code or configuration changes. Risk teams spend their time on judgment calls and policy design, and the bank can show regulators the same evidence it uses for its own decisions.

The same foundation extends further. Continuous reassessment keeps evidence aligned with a changing code base after launch. New regulations can be encoded once as checks and applied across every use case. Aggregated scores give boards an enterprise-wide view of AI risk instead of a collection of individual reviews.

According to recent reports, for any institution scaling AI, the question worth asking is how many of its policies have ever been tested against a running system. Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Sets for Incomplete Data

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (248 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31329v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Attribute reduction in incomplete information systems is difficult because missing values break the equivalence-class structure of rough set theory. We propose the Conservative Overlap Fuzzy Rough Set (COFRS) model. Each object is described by its set of present attributes. The similarity of two objects is a weighted overlap on the attributes present in both, divided by the fixed number of attributes |A| instead of the size of their union, so missing values are penalised globally and are not matched as wildcards. From this similarity we define a soft dependency degree based on weighted granule consistency, and we search for reducts by greedy backward elimination in O(|U|^2 |A|^2) time. We show that the relation is symmetric and non-reflexive, that the dependency degree is not monotone, and we give a sufficient condition under which monotonicity holds. On 11 UCI benchmarks with missing rates from 0.15% to 20.46%, COFRS gives the smallest reducts on average (4.1 attributes, against 5.0-11.2 for Tolerance-RS, a range-threshold variant Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and the min-aggregation variant COFRS-min). The difference is significant against Tol-RS_tau, Zhou-RS and COFRS-min (Holm-adjusted Wilcoxon p<0.01) but not against Tolerance-RS (p=0.56), and it is small against the Jensen-Shen selector (adjusted p=0.084). At equal reduct size, COFRS selects more informative attributes than random subsets. With a kNN classifier the methods do not differ significantly in accuracy, F1 or G-mean; with an RBF-SVM they do, and COFRS ranks last. The gain is therefore compactness, not predictive accuracy.

Sources indicate that arXiv:2611.34099v1 Announce Type: newly introduced Abstract: How does task complexity shape firms' willingness to substitute entry-level labour with artificial intelligence (AI) tools? We study this question using a pre-registered survey experiment with managers from 1,435 German firms in the information economy and manufacturing industry. Managers are randomly assigned to consider a long lasting need for additional capacity involving either well-structured and standardised tasks, or more complex tasks that require professional judgement, contextual knowledge and independent problem-solving. Relative to standardised tasks, complex tasks reduce willingness to use AI rather than hire an entry-level employee by 0.54 points on a five-point scale and increase the importance attached to human oversight by 0.15 points. Further, pre-treatment responses indicate that managers expect the availability of AI applications to reduce hiring of both entry-level employees and experienced workers, but significantly more strongly for entry-level workers.

#10154. The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

The Definitive Fine-Tuning Guide for 3D Generation Models

📅 12 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 13 min read (2611 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Hugging Face

⏱️ ~13 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Recent findings suggest that TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs.
  • According to recent reports, 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment.
  • Sources indicate that TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Recent findings suggest that TLDR; In this blog, we provide fine-tuning scripts and containers to fine-tune TRELLIS.2, a popular 3D model on your 3D assets, that can run both locally and on Hugging Face Jobs. If you are interested in fine-tuning, you can use our scripts with few arguments (assuming you updated your dataset to Hugging Face Hub) or tinker with them yourself with this repository. If you want to learn more, we go through how the script works. Let’s go!

According to recent reports, 3D generation has many uses in robotics, simulation, media, and entertainment. In these fields, it is difficult to make generated objects obey strict rules and standardize model and data representations. There are many file formats, such as GLB and PLY. There are also many representations, such as neural radiance fields (NeRFs) and 3D Gaussian splatting (3DGS). Each one has different advantages and disadvantages.

Sources indicate that TRELLIS introduced a common internal representation, called a unified latent representation. Its decoders convert this representation into 3D models in the required output format. Thus, you do not have to use different models for each representation format.

The same team then released TRELLIS.2, which improves the model's representation of 3D structure. But neither model gives an easy way to adapt it to a specific task.

A general-purpose model, such as TRELLIS.2, can make errors in details that are important for a specific application. For example, a user may need accurate geometry for furniture models. Without fine-tuning for that task, the pretrained model can produce geometry that is insufficiently accurate. We use a subset of GSO that has 188 footwear objects for our experiment. In our initial tests, the pretrained model usually produced shoes that looked correct, but the soles were incorrect. We test whether a LoRA can make the soles more accurate.

Our goal is to use the Google Scanned Objects (GSO) dataset to improve the performance of TRELLIS.2 on a specific object category. We will explain which pipeline components to fine-tune and which to leave unchanged during training. The pipeline separates structure, detailed geometry, and materials. Thus, we will fine-tune only the components that are important for our task.

Choosing what to freeze matters as much as choosing what to fine-tune.

Recent findings suggest that loRA, short for low-rank adaptation, fine-tunes a model by training small adapter matrices while keeping the original weights frozen. This reduces the number of trainable parameters and the memory needed for their gradients and optimizer state. We use Hugging Face’s PEFT library to add and train these adapters. For more information, read our LoRA guide.

Recent findings suggest that hugging Face Jobs runs containerized workloads on cloud hardware. We use it for preprocessing and for training. To use your own GPU instead, see the local Docker commands below. Before you start, make sure that you have:.

Before we train, let’s look at how TRELLIS.2 generates a 3D object and where we’ll add LoRA adapters.

Industry observers note that TRELLIS.2 has five main stages: remove the image background, encode the image, predict the coarse structure, generate detailed geometry, and generate materials. The pipeline then exports the result as a textured mesh.

First, BiRefNet removes the background from the input image. DINOv3-L then encodes the image into feature tokens. The generation models use these tokens to guide the 3D object.

Industry observers note that the sparse-structure flow DiT predicts the object's coarse shape. It is a diffusion transformer (DiT) that makes a small latent of size 16³ × 8. A variational autoencoder (VAE) decoder then changes this latent into a 64 × 64 × 64 occupancy grid. Each voxel in the grid demonstrates if that location is part of the object. A voxel is a pixel in three dimensions. We add LoRA adapters to this model because its output guides the geometry stage.

O-Voxel is the 3D format of TRELLIS.2. It is a sparse voxel grid. It keeps only the voxels on the object's surface. Each voxel keeps local geometry, such as a mesh vertex, and material attributes. Because the format is small, a CPU changes a mesh into O-Voxel in seconds. A GPU changes O-Voxel back into a mesh in seconds.

Sources indicate that structured sparse latents come from TRELLIS. They keep 3D data in sparse tensors, which makes computation faster. The model uses only approximately 10% of the voxels in the grid, so it does not spend compute on empty voxels. Thus, the shape flow DiT and the texture flow DiT are sparse transformers. The sparse-structure flow DiT is a dense transformer.

Industry observers note that the shape flow DiT uses the occupancy grid and the DINOv3 feature tokens to make a latent. Another VAE decoder then changes this latent into O-Voxel geometry at a resolution of 512 × 512 × 512.

We add LoRA adapters to the DiT at this stage because it controls the object's shape.

Recent findings suggest that in the last stage, the texture flow DiT uses the shape latent and the DINOv3 features as input. It defines the materials and textures of the geometry's surface. A VAE decoder then changes the latent into base color, metallic, roughness, and alpha values for each voxel. We do not add LoRA adapters to this stage. Our dataset has diffuse color maps, but it lacks the separate material maps this stage needs for training. Also, our problem is the shoe's shape. The base model already makes good colors and textures.

Finally, the pipeline combines the geometry and material attributes into a textured mesh and exports it as a GLB file.

Recent findings suggest that we add LoRA adapters only to the sparse-structure flow DiT and the shape flow DiT. These DiTs control the object's shape and geometry. We freeze the texture flow DiT to keep its current capabilities.

In a recent development, our dataset contains diffuse color maps that include baked lighting effects. To train the texture flow DiT, we need separate material maps. The color maps in our dataset mix surface color with lighting. Thus, they are not correct targets for this training.

If we train the texture flow DiT on these maps, it can learn to show lighting as a surface property. It can also forget what it learned before, a problem called catastrophic forgetting.

Our subset has 188 shoes from the 1,030 objects in GSO. For a dataset this small, LoRA is a better choice than full fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning costs much more. It can also overwrite what the model already does well (its learned priors). Our configuration trains approximately 9.3 million adapter parameters in total for both targeted DiTs. We use rank 8 adapters in the attention and feed-forward (MLP) layers of the sparse-structure flow DiT. We use rank 16 adapters in the attention layers of the shape flow DiT. The rank sets the size of the adapter matrices. A higher rank lets the adapter learn more.

In a recent development, A 3D model setup can need many dependencies and installation steps. We supply two Docker images (that you can run on Jobs or your own machine) with the necessary software. One image is for preprocessing, and one is for fine-tuning.

To train your LoRA adapters and upload them to the Hub:.

Then we explain the fine-tuning script, its settings, and how each setting affects training.

We’ll walk through three parts of the experiment:.

We save the preprocessed dataset so that all training runs can reuse it.

The preprocessing container uses Blender to render 16 views of each object. LoRA training will use these views as conditioning images. Blender runs without a display, through the xvfb-run utility. The container also processes each object through the preprocessing pipeline. See the footwear dataset here for an example intermediate output. For our 188 objects, the full run took approximately 1 hour on an a100-large job. A compact version of the preprocessing pipeline is also available in this companion repository.

For Hugging Face Jobs, we pass the following arguments:.

Sources indicate that this container accepts a few more arguments (regardless of being run on Hugging Face Jobs or with Docker), that you can find documented over here. The steps taken in the preprocessing pipeline are documented in this section later.

Industry observers note that the training container loads the prepared dataset and a configuration preset or file. It records training metrics with Trackio. Use the Trackio dashboard to monitor the run.

In a recent development, we use ‘ss’ and ‘shape’ to indicate the two modes we have for training the LoRAs. The ‘ss’ mode will finetune only the Sparse-Structure Flow DiT, whereas the ‘shape’ mode will finetune the Shape Flow DiT. Under the hood, they simply reference different config.json files to use for each stage. More details about the process is available in this section later.

Sources indicate that if you set --push-to, the container uploads adapter checkpoints to the Hub. The container accepts parameters that are also documented here for brevity. A compact script is also available in the same repository.

If you want to play around and fine-tune with the already-processed dataset we have, feel free to use the following set of commands.

Recent findings suggest that the commands and flags are the same as for Hugging Face Jobs. Only the Docker options are different.

If you want to use our already-preprocessed dataset locally on your machine of choice, use the following commands:.

Our trained LoRA adapters are in this repository: suvadityamuk/trellis-2-finetune-gso.

We use TRELLIS.2’s frozen encoders to convert the input meshes into training latents. We save these latents, so later runs do not have to encode the meshes again.

We also render 16 views of each object in Blender. During training, we select one random view for each sample as the conditioning image. We keep 9 of the 188 objects for evaluation and train on the other 179. These held-out objects show whether the adapters work on objects unseen by the model during training.

Some of the views that Blender rendered for one object.

The first snippet sets up the data. FLOW selects the flow DiT to train (ss or shape), and STEPS sets the number of optimizer steps. A batch size of 4 with 4 gradient accumulation steps gives an effective batch size of 16. Then, the snippet loads the LoRA config file for the selected flow DiT, makes the dataset in the TRELLIS.2 format, removes the held-out objects, and makes the data loader for fine-tuning.

We use the peft library to insert LoRA adapters into the selected layers. TRELLIS.2 has a custom forward pass, so the standard PeftModel() wrapper does not work. Instead, we call inject_adapter_in_model(). This function adds the adapters directly to the model and keeps its custom interface.

We keep the trainable adapter weights in 32-bit floating point (fp32) for numerical stability and use bfloat16 (bf16) autocasting for the forward pass. Autocasting lets PyTorch use lower precision for some operations, which decreases memory use. Autocasting does not change how the frozen backbone weights are stored.

Industry observers note that it’s notable to note that our objective function here is good-old rectified flow matching (as seen in popular image-generation models like Stable Diffusion 3, Flux 2, and others). TRELLIS.2 used the same objective in pretraining, so it is a good choice for fine-tuning. For the theory, read this blog about flow matching.

We patch only the LoRA parameters in the sparse-structure and shape DiTs. All original model weights remain frozen.

The snippets below show the core training loop for one stage. They are simpler than the container code and do not include some setup steps. For the full workflow, use the container commands.

We initialize the optimizer and load DINOv3 to extract features from the input images.

We then follow these steps within the training loop:.

The training loop computes the loss and updates the adapter weights. Gradient accumulation adds the gradients from 4 small batches before each optimizer step. Gradient checkpointing saves GPU memory by recomputing some intermediate values during backpropagation. The outer loop runs for a given number of optimizer steps, whereas the inner loop accumulates gradients over a set of batches.

Sources indicate that for each batch, DINOv3 encodes the conditioning image. For classifier-free guidance (CFG) dropout, the loop sets the conditioning to zero for a random fraction (p_uncond) of the samples. Then, it calculates the flow-matching loss with bf16 autocasting. After the inner loop, it clips the gradients to prevent very large updates and does an optimizer step. It logs the loss every 10 steps and saves an adapter checkpoint every 500 steps.

We trained two adapters: one for the sparse-structure DiT and one for the shape DiT. The LoRA config files in the container image contain the full training settings: ss_flow_lora_gso.json for the sparse-structure flow DiT and slat_flow_img2shape_lora_gso.json for the shape flow DiT. Each run used one A100 80 GB on Hugging Face Jobs. The sparse-structure run took 7.2 hours, and the shape run took 3.6 hours.

Recent findings suggest that the training loss of the sparse-structure flow DiT falls rapidly at the start, then more slowly. The loss of the shape flow DiT stays at approximately the same level. These curves show how the training objective changes, but they do not directly measure the quality of the generated geometry.

It has been revealed that flow-matching loss varies with the sampled objects, noise, and timesteps. To find out if fine-tuning improves the geometry, we must also compare outputs on the held-out objects.

The figure below compares outputs for five of the nine held-out objects. It demonstrates the input image, the base model’s generated output, the base output after a rotation adjustment, the output with the footwear adapters, and the reference scan. In these examples, the soles from the fine-tuned model are closer to the scans.

We also use three metrics to evaluate the geometry on the test set:.

In the chart’s nine-object comparison, the base model has a mean F-score of 0.276, compared with 0.803 for the model with the footwear adapters. Chamfer distance falls from 0.174 to 0.033, and normal consistency rises from 0.530 to 0.804. With both adapters, the F-score is better on all nine held-out objects.

For the statistics of all runs, see this Trackio space.

According to recent reports, phew, so there we go! We fine-tuned TRELLIS.2 for footwear generation by adding LoRA adapters to the two model components that control geometry. We prepared the data once, trained the adapters in separate jobs, and evaluated the outputs on held-out objects.

The main lesson is to select a training target that agrees with the problem and the data that you have. For this experiment, we fine-tuned the structure and shape stages and froze the texture stage.

Next, we can examine if the same choices help other 3D generation models, such as Pixal3D and UniLat3D.

Recent findings suggest that gaussian-splat and world-generation models, such as HunyuanWorld 2.0 and NVIDIA Lyra 2.0, are also possible next steps. Their representations and training pipelines can need different methods.

In a recent development, thank you for following along, and see you in the next one! 👋🤗.

An interesting application of LoRA for adapting models to specialized 3D generation tasks. It demonstrates how parameter-efficient training can make model customization more accessible without requiring the resources associated with full fine-tuning. Understanding the differences between LoRA, full fine-tuning, and other adaptation strategies is crucial when selecting an approach for a particular use case. This guide on LLM fine-tuning techniques provides additional insights into these methods and their trade-offs.

MOZAIC: An Audio-Video Deepfake Benchmark for Telling What Is Fake

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (214 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2611.31301v2 Announce Type: new Abstract: Audio-video (AV) deepfakes can fake the face, the voice, or both. Most benchmarks only ask whether a clip is real or fake, so they cannot show whether a detector relies on the picture, the voice, or encoding traces. We present MOZAIC, a paired benchmark with a 4-way label in which every source clip is released in all four combinations of real or fake video and real or fake audio so each modality contribution can be measured directly. Fakes cover inner-face swapping, whole-frame video diffusion and voice conversion. MOZAIC has 137,745 clips from 15,014 source pairs and four tasks: T1 AV authenticity, T2 manipulation type, T3 identity verification and T4 explanation. We evaluate 12 AV multimodal LLMs (MLLMs), train four detectors and fine-tune MLLMs with LoRA. Overall, the best MLLM reaches only 35.6% on the four-way T1 and catches far more video-only fakes than voice-only fakes (43.6% vs 7.5%). Trained detectors reach 98.4% on T1, and LoRA fine-tuning raises explanation scores (OmniVinci 4.17 to 7.40, Qwen2.5-Omni 4.42 to 6.98), but the best T1 detector falls to 78.3% when the face-swap generator is held out of training, so generalization and explanation remain open. We release the dataset, the compact MOZAIC-SMALL split, the code and the prompts. https://vectorinstitute.github.io/mozaic/.
